## DAILY SECURITY BRIEF

### 1. CIA director reportedly made an unannounced Moscow visit
U.S. media reported that CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow on Aug. 25 for undisclosed meetings with Russian officials. Washington reportedly asked Ukraine to suspend strikes on Moscow and St. Petersburg during the visit; Kyiv agreed. Neither government has confirmed the agenda.

**Why it matters:** The first known visit by a CIA director to Moscow since 2021 indicates that high-level intelligence channels remain active despite stalled Ukraine negotiations. The talks may also have involved detainees, NATO security concerns or Iran, but these possibilities remain unconfirmed.

### 2. Ukraine moves toward domestic production of Western cruise missiles
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Britain and France had approved steps enabling Ukraine to produce Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles domestically, including sharing protected technical information. Ukraine also reported receiving a small number of additional Patriot interceptors and AIM missiles, with future Crotale air-defense deliveries confirmed.

**Why it matters:** Domestic missile production could strengthen Ukraine’s long-range strike capacity and reduce dependence on individual deliveries. However, the limited number of new Patriot interceptors underscores continuing shortages in defense against Russian ballistic missiles.

### 3. Fighting remains intense as Ukrainian strikes pressure Russian energy infrastructure
Ukraine’s General Staff reported 203 combat engagements and extensive Russian use of aircraft and drones on Aug. 25, with the heaviest assaults around Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka. Separately, Ukrainian attacks reportedly struck Russian refining and gas-processing facilities. Russia is expected to extend restrictions on diesel exports amid refinery outages and domestic fuel shortages.

**Why it matters:** The battlefield remains highly attritional, while Ukraine’s campaign against Russian energy infrastructure is producing measurable economic and logistical pressure. Moscow has also broadened state authority to take temporary control of companies deemed insufficiently protected against drone attacks.

### 4. Washington shifts toward intensified economic pressure on Iran
The United States announced expanded secondary sanctions targeting more than 60 individuals, companies and vessels linked to Iranian oil revenue, weapons procurement, cyber activity and financial networks. Shipping, aviation, technology, gold and digital assets are also targeted. Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly told allies that new U.S. strikes were not expected for the time being.

**Why it matters:** The measures signal a shift from direct military action toward economic coercion after six months of inconclusive conflict. Enforcement against Iran’s trading networks—particularly those connected to China and the UAE—could widen diplomatic and financial friction.

### 5. Syria and Israel resume senior-level security contact
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and Mossad chief Roman Gofman met in Jordan under U.S. mediation, in the highest-level publicly announced direct contact in the current security track. Discussions reportedly covered de-escalation, Israeli attacks and arrests, security zones in southern Syria, and possible renewed negotiations.

**Why it matters:** The meeting reopens a diplomatic channel after an Israeli strike disrupted contacts. Major obstacles remain, including Israeli-held Syrian territory, Damascus’s defense relationship with Turkey and disagreement over Syrian military deployments.

## WATCH

- **Ratcliffe visit:** Any official disclosure of participants or outcomes, particularly signs of renewed Ukraine negotiations or U.S.-Russian intelligence coordination.
- **Russian strategic weapons:** OSINT indicators suggest preparations on Novaya Zemlya for another test of the nuclear-powered Burevestnik cruise missile; monitor for a launch and radiation reporting.
- **Iran escalation risks:** Enforcement of secondary sanctions, Iranian activity around the Strait of Hormuz and whether pressure on Chinese or Gulf-based trade networks triggers retaliation.

### India and China Resume High-Level Border Dialogue

Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi held the 25th round of talks under their countries’ special-representative border mechanism in Beijing. Discussions covered stability along the disputed Himalayan frontier and broader economic, political and multilateral cooperation. Both sides described bilateral relations as gradually normalizing after the deadly 2020 Ladakh clash.

**Why it matters:** Sustained border engagement could reduce the risk of confrontation between two nuclear-armed powers. Improved ties may also enable greater trade, investment and diplomatic coordination, although India continues to make wider normalization conditional on peace along the frontier.

### China Avoids Criticizing North Korean Missile Barrage

North Korea launched more than 10 short-range ballistic missiles shortly after Wang Yi concluded a visit to South Korea. Seoul and Tokyo condemned the launches, while Beijing said only that it had noted the reports and offered no further comment. Analysts assessed that China remains more focused on preserving stability in North Korea than on pressing Pyongyang toward near-term denuclearization.

**Why it matters:** Beijing’s response highlights the limits of its willingness to restrain North Korea despite engaging diplomatically with Seoul. Continued missile activity could increase pressure on South Korea and Japan to deepen defense cooperation with the United States.

### North Korea Intensifies Anti-Japan Messaging

North Korean state media has issued repeated denunciations of Japan, accusing Tokyo of reviving militarism and preparing for aggression. The sharper rhetoric coincides with North Korea’s expanding security and economic ties with Russia and Japan’s efforts to strengthen its defense posture.

**Why it matters:** The messaging reinforces an increasingly polarized regional environment involving North Korea, Russia and China on one side and Japan and its partners on the other. It may also foreshadow further North Korean military demonstrations aimed at Japan.

### WATCH

- Whether India-China border talks produce concrete disengagement or confidence-building measures.
- Further North Korean missile tests and any change in China’s diplomatic response or Japan’s defense posture.
regional_summaries.europe_russia:
### Ukraine moves toward domestic production of Western cruise missiles

President Volodymyr Zelensky said Britain and France had approved steps allowing Ukraine to produce Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles domestically, including the sharing of classified technical information and lifting of licensing restrictions. Ukraine also reported receiving additional Patriot and AIM interceptors and commitments for several Crotale air-defense systems.

**Why it matters:** Domestic missile production could strengthen Ukraine’s capacity for sustained precision strikes while reducing dependence on individual foreign deliveries. The additional air-defense munitions address an urgent requirement, although Zelensky said the number of new Patriot interceptors remained small.

### CIA director reportedly holds unannounced Moscow talks

Multiple media outlets reported that CIA Director John Ratcliffe visited Moscow on August 25 for meetings with senior Russian officials. Neither government disclosed the agenda or officially confirmed the talks. The United States reportedly asked Ukraine to suspend strikes on Moscow and St. Petersburg during the visit, and Kyiv complied.

**Why it matters:** The visit represents a rare high-level US-Russian contact amid stalled negotiations over Ukraine. It could involve war-related diplomacy, intelligence communication or detainee issues, but the absence of official information leaves its purpose uncertain.

### Ukrainian strikes intensify pressure on Russia’s energy sector

Ukraine reported further attacks on Russian refineries and energy facilities, including the Afipsky refinery and the Astrakhan gas-processing plant. Reuters sources said Russia was preparing to extend restrictions on diesel exports as domestic shortages persisted. Separately, President Vladimir Putin authorized temporary state management of broadly defined critical infrastructure when owners are judged to have provided inadequate protection against drone attacks.

**Why it matters:** Continued disruption of refining and fuel distribution could constrain Russian export revenue and complicate domestic and military logistics. The new decree also gives the Russian state wide discretion to assume control of private assets, increasing regulatory and ownership risks for major businesses.

### WATCH

- **Possible Burevestnik test:** Aircraft and maritime deployments around Novaya Zemlya indicate Russia may be preparing another test of its nuclear-powered cruise missile.  
- **Russia-NATO security tensions:** Monitor suspected sabotage targeting European military-logistics infrastructure and Russian rhetoric concerning British defense manufacturers supporting Ukraine.
regional_summaries.middle_east:
## 1. US shifts Iran strategy toward intensified economic pressure

**What happened:** Washington announced expanded secondary sanctions targeting Iran’s oil-related networks, shipping, aviation, technology, gold and digital-asset sectors, as well as roughly 60 individuals, companies and vessels. US officials indicated that renewed military strikes were not expected in the immediate term. Pakistan separately reported constructive mediation efforts, while Iran and Oman discussed a temporary, mine-cleared navigation corridor through the Strait of Hormuz.

**Why it matters:** The measures signal a shift from direct military action toward economic coercion after months of stalemate. Their effectiveness will depend heavily on enforcement against Iran’s trading partners, particularly Chinese oil buyers. Continued restrictions in Hormuz remain a major threat to global energy supplies, shipping costs and regional stability.

## 2. Syria and Israel resume high-level security contact

**What happened:** Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani met Israeli Mossad chief Roman Gofman in Jordan in talks mediated by the United States. Damascus said discussions covered de-escalation, Israeli military operations and arrests, and the possible revival of negotiations on security arrangements in southern Syria. Syria is seeking an Israeli withdrawal from territory captured after the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s government.

**Why it matters:** The meeting was the highest-level publicly acknowledged direct contact in the current security track. It could reopen negotiations on buffer zones and force deployments, but major differences remain over Syrian sovereignty, Israel’s security demands and Syria’s military and foreign relationships.

## 3. Gaza ceasefire faces renewed strain

**What happened:** The US-led body overseeing the Gaza peace plan warned Hamas to halt militant activity, including kite launches, after Israel threatened additional operations. The body also said Israel must limit military action to genuine and imminent threats. Separately, residents said an Israeli strike destroyed a nearly completed desalination facility in northern Gaza; Israel said it targeted a Hamas weapons depot in the area.

**Why it matters:** The exchanges demonstrate the ceasefire’s fragility and the risk that relatively limited incidents could trigger broader retaliation. Damage to civilian infrastructure also compounds Gaza’s humanitarian crisis and may complicate implementation of later stages of the peace plan.

## WATCH

- **Strait of Hormuz:** Monitor whether Iran and Oman establish the proposed corridor, whether shipping volumes recover, and whether further tanker incidents occur.
- **Yemen–Saudi tensions:** Ansar Allah claimed attacks on a Saudi oil tanker and Saudi-linked military targets. Independent confirmation and any Saudi response will be important indicators of possible escalation.
regional_summaries.america_other:
## 1. SOUTHCOM Expands Lethal Counter-Cartel Operations

U.S. Southern Command conducted its first lethal strike under the permanent Joint Task Force-Western Hemisphere, targeting a suspected drug-trafficking vessel in the eastern Pacific. Two alleged traffickers were killed. Separately, the United States is reportedly preparing to transfer three MQ-9 Reaper drones to Colombia, likely accompanied by training and operational support.

**Why it matters:** The developments indicate deeper U.S. military involvement in regional counter-narcotics operations, including direct strikes and expanded intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance cooperation with Colombia. They could increase pressure on cartels but also raise sovereignty, legal and civilian-protection concerns.

## 2. Colombia and Venezuela Reopen Channels with Israel

Venezuela revived consular services with Israel, although it has not restored full diplomatic relations. Colombia reportedly moved further by restoring diplomatic and security cooperation, recognizing Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights and considering closer defense ties.

**Why it matters:** These moves would reverse previous policies of distancing from Israel and could reshape Latin American diplomatic alignments. Renewed Colombian security cooperation may also create opportunities for Israeli arms, drone and technology sales.

## 3. United States Moves to Expand Long-Range Strike Capacity

The U.S. Navy awarded Castelion nearly $90 million to advance 50 Blackbeard hypersonic weapons toward early operational capability, including modifications intended to facilitate exports. Separately, Raytheon reportedly received a seven-year, $22.9 billion contract aimed at raising Tomahawk missile production above 1,000 annually for the U.S. Navy and allied customers.

**Why it matters:** The investments signal an effort to expand inventories of long-range precision weapons and reduce dependence on small numbers of costly systems. Higher production could strengthen U.S. deterrence and improve the availability of missiles for allies, provided supply chains can meet the planned targets.

## WATCH

- Whether the reported MQ-9 transfer to Colombia proceeds, and what operational restrictions or U.S. support accompany it.
- Whether Venezuela restores full relations with Israel and whether Colombia’s renewed ties produce major defense procurements.

articles.title: Hackers published a ‘Sberbank memo’ war-gaming eight endings to the war in Ukraine. One source in Russia’s financial market thinks a chatbot wrote it.
articles.body:
Hackers published a ‘Sberbank memo’ war-gaming eight endings to the war in Ukraine. One source in Russia’s financial market thinks a chatbot wrote it.
The hacker group Black Mirror has published screenshots of a purported Sberbank analytical memo that lists eight scenarios for ending the full-scale war between Russia and Ukraine. The document is dated April 2026, meaning it was prepared before Ukrainian forces stepped up strikes on oil refineries and logistics sites. According to the hackers, the memo came from correspondence between Sberbank board chairman German Gref and an unnamed correspondent. The authenticity of the screenshots has not been confirmed, and it is not known who wrote the memo. Sberbank has not commented on the reported leak of the correspondence. Meduza runs through the scenarios outlined in the document.
Update: A source in Russia’s financial sector told Meduza that they had not seen the original of the “memo” but suspected the material was generated by an AI chatbot. That theory is backed up by Pangram, an AI-detection service, which found that 83% of the document’s English-language text was machine-generated.
1. Russia’s decisive military advantage
Probability: 7%
This scenario envisions Russia gaining full control over the four “new constituent entities” — the self-proclaimed Donetsk People’s Republic (“DPR”), the self-proclaimed Luhansk People’s Republic (“LPR”), Zaporizhzhia region, and Kherson region — within their administrative borders. The document also mentions Kharkiv region as a kind of “political symbol.” It does not contemplate taking Kyiv, but Russia would have to force Ukraine into talks “from a position of absolute military dominance.”
The document says Russia cannot carry this out without a second wave of mobilization — 300,000 to 500,000 people. Under current conditions, contract soldiers are enough to replace Russia’s monthly losses of 20,000 to 25,000 troops, but not enough to build new strike groups. The country would also need to fix its rear-area air defenses, since Ukrainian strikes on oil and military facilities — including strikes with “Flamingo” missiles — could make the cost of an offensive “unacceptable” for Russia.
Analysts also point to the need to increase air support several times over and to field autonomous drone swarms coordinated by artificial intelligence. The document says Western software could help Ukraine do this faster.
Another important point:
- Analysts at the Russian state bank Sberbank put Vladimir Putin’s real approval rating at 55% to 65%. Mobilization could cut that by another 10 to 15 percentage points, and only a guaranteed successful offensive would offset the decline.
2. ‘Exhaustion of the West’: peace on Russia’s terms
Probability: 12%
In this scenario, Ukraine loses political — and with it, financial — support from its Western allies. That would require three factors to coincide: U.S. support for Ukraine falling below 30%, an energy crisis in Europe this coming winter, and a domestic political crisis in Ukraine itself.
Russia could then secure the lifting of some sanctions and guarantees that Ukraine will not join NATO. Analysts consider each of these three factors likely on its own but doubt all three will occur at once.
The conflict would be frozen without a formal treaty, and Ukraine could still join the European Union. The document draws a comparison to Cyprus, which does not control all of its own territory: Northern Cyprus is under Turkish control and recognized by no country other than Turkey, yet the Republic of Cyprus remains an EU member.
Another important point:
- Sberbank estimates that, as of April 2026, Russia’s economy can hold out for another 12 to 18 months under current conditions. Analysts say time favors Russia, since every month that passes weakens the Western coalition.
3. ‘Trump’s deal’: a frozen conflict with partial sanctions relief
Probability: 32%
This scenario resembles the previous one but, in Sberbank’s view, is more likely. The conflict freezes, most likely without a formal peace treaty; Ukraine does not join NATO; and some sanctions are lifted. The United States accepts Russian control over the four regions while still legally recognizing Ukraine’s 1991 borders. The EU does not recognize the new borders.
Analysts put the scenario’s probability high because they expect Donald Trump to want a deal closed before the November 2026 midterm elections, which would push him to pressure both sides. He would threaten Russia with lifting all restrictions on arming Ukraine, and Ukraine with cutting off support entirely. A successful deal would let Trump stake a claim to the Nobel Peace Prize.
The problem: neither side trusts Trump’s long-term guarantees, and any change in the U.S. administration could reignite the conflict. A durable deal would require a multilateral format, but Trump shuns such arrangements, and European countries would oppose the deal.
Another important point:
- For Russia, this scenario would amount to neither victory nor defeat. The document says the Kremlin could sell the deal at home as “forcing NATO to retreat,” which would boost its approval rating. But an unfinished war could also fuel opposition sentiment.
4. A ‘Korean freeze’: without a formal agreement
Probability: 22%
This scenario would play out if neither side could achieve a decisive breakthrough. The conflict fades without a formal agreement, the front line stabilizes, and the intensity of fighting declines — though the drone war continues.
Analysts say this is possible if Trump loses interest in Ukraine and turns his attention to another country or to domestic politics. The EU would then shoulder the bulk of support for Ukraine and speed up the country’s accession to the union.
For Russia, this would mean not just a “normalization of the war” but an economic respite as well. Sberbank says the risks to those in power are relatively low: the ruling party United Russia’s low approval rating — 31% — points to war fatigue, but analysts see no revolutionary potential in it.
Another important point:
- Both sides could use the pause to rearm on a large scale over the following three to five years. The next stage of the conflict would be a technologically different war altogether.
5. A protracted war (another two to three years)
Probability: 15%
The conflict grinds on without a freeze or breakthroughs, with Russian losses and front-line advances holding at current levels. This scenario would mean a total failure of diplomacy.
Ukraine would face a humanitarian catastrophe and demographic collapse. Russia would be forced to fight “at the outer limit of what its economy can bear,” though analysts do not expect significant protests at first. Birth rates would continue to fall, and skilled workers would keep leaving the country, while Putin’s real approval rating would fall below 50%.
At some point, the Russian public might break its silence — something that would happen if living standards fell noticeably, as they did during perestroika from 1986 to 1991.
Another important point:
- This scenario implies a further tightening of sanctions. Russia’s isolation would continue to grow, though it would not reach the level of Iran or North Korea, since the country would still be trading with China, India, and others.
6. Peace on compromise terms
Probability: 5%
Significant political change on one side of the conflict could lead to a full-fledged peace treaty with mutual concessions. Analysts doubt, though, that Putin’s position will weaken substantially — they are more inclined to bet on a change of power in Ukraine or on outside pressure on both sides, including from China on Russia.
Under this scenario, Russia could return part of the occupied territory to Ukraine — Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions in part, or all previously captured territories — in exchange for recognition of Russian control over Crimea and part of the Donbas. Ukraine would get security guarantees and the possibility of joining the EU and even NATO, though not sooner than 15 to 25 years from now.
This would be the most difficult scenario for both sides. Ukraine would effectively be forced into capitulation, while Russia would have to explain to its own population what the war — which cost hundreds of thousands of lives — was actually for.
Another important point:
- Russia would also have to overhaul its current narrative. It has written the “four new constituent entities” into its constitution, which would make returning any of that territory politically very difficult.
7. Peace on Ukraine’s and Europe’s terms
Probability: 2%
Sberbank rates this the least likely scenario of all: Russia withdraws to the 2014 or 1991 borders and pays reparations, while Ukraine joins NATO. Crimea would either be returned to Ukraine or become the subject of negotiations.
Such an outcome could follow from an economic collapse in Russia (GDP falling by more than 15%, hyperinflation), a catastrophic military defeat, or regime change. Analysts consider all three unlikely.
Another important point:
- The document says this outcome would require the eighth and final scenario to unfold — and analysts currently see no preconditions for that.
8. The ‘wild card’: black swans
Probability: 5% (combined for all sub-variants)
Here, Sberbank considers unlikely events that could radically alter the course of the conflict. None of the possibilities below can be forecast using standard analytical methods.
Nuclear escalation: Russia’s use of tactical nuclear weapons. This would bring instant and total isolation, cutting Russia off from Chinese and Indian support — and could also draw a NATO response.
“A new Chernobyl”: a Russian strike on a nuclear facility such as the Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant or the Chernobyl sarcophagus. Such a strike would set off a humanitarian catastrophe on a scale that would eclipse either side’s war aims, and international pressure would force an immediate ceasefire.
A direct NATO–Russia clash: a provocation — in the Baltic Sea, for example — or an incident involving a missile or drone on NATO territory. A series of such incidents or a deliberate strike would escalate into direct conflict.
Regime change: Putin’s removal from power by the security services in order to make peace, or Ukraine’s military leadership putting forward an alternative to Volodymyr Zelensky. The document says a change of power in Russia is unlikely: “Prigozhin has been eliminated, Shoigu has been transferred, Surkov has been removed.”
An Iranian cascade: a new round of conflict in the Middle East involving the United States, Iran, Israel, and other countries. It would sharply increase Russia’s oil revenues, trigger an energy crisis in Europe, and push Ukraine further down the Western agenda.
A technological surprise: a breakthrough in AI-assisted drone swarm control, or a cyberattack on critical infrastructure in Russia or Ukraine. The first would hand one side an absolute tactical advantage; the second would strip its target of the ability to wage war.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: With no friends left to burn, Trump is running out of diplomatic ammunition | Rafael Behr
articles.body:
Now is the twilight of Donald Trump’s supremacy. The US is still the richest and most heavily armed nation on Earth. That status is secure. The current president, contemptuous of law and indulged in lawlessness by a supine Congress, enjoys even greater power than the constitution allows.
With those advantages it takes a special talent for incompetence to look as thwarted and impotent as Trump does with more than two years of his second term still to run.
History will record the war against Iran as a turning point in the fortunes of the current US administration and a grievous wound to national prestige.
Pumped with hubris after the audacious military operation to kidnap Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro, Trump believed an equally brisk triumph was available in the Middle East. The Tehran regime would be decapitated. The country’s hydrocarbon resources would then be available for US exploitation.
Six months later, Iran is controlled by a new generation of hardliners. Emboldened by resilience under US and Israeli bombardment, they demand financial concessions from Washington as the price for peace – reparations and a right to toll the strait of Hormuz.
The war is not over, it has just turned cold. Trump believes Iran’s fragile economy is close to collapse. He threatens to push it over the brink with “D-day” sanctions. The metaphor of second world war amphibious assault is supposed to make yet another round of financial coercion succeed where past embargos have failed.
It is true that ordinary Iranians are suffering terrible privations, but repression limits their capacity to translate discontent into demands for political change. By contrast, US consumers, aggrieved by the inflationary consequences of the war, and confused about its purpose, get to express their unhappiness in midterm elections in November.
The calculation in Tehran is that American tolerance for economic pain is low enough that Trump will be forced to blink first. It is a reasonable assumption: the need to declare mission accomplished to a domestic audience – even on terms that amount to defeat by any objective measure – drive an impatient president’s actions more than long-term strategy.
If sanctions fail, diplomatic climbdown is the only remaining move. The Pentagon couldn’t revert to the all-out military option even if Trump ordered it, because Operation Epic Fury burned too much of the national munitions stockpile.
This is where an asymmetry of cost and capability comes into play. Iran can frighten ships out of the Gulf with a few mines. It can harry neighbouring states with drones knocked together for less than $50,000 and dispatched from mobile launchers that are hard to target. The Patriot interceptors that protect US forces and their allies in the region cost $4-5m apiece. (More than 1,500 Patriots are thought have been fired in the war so far, leaving fewer than 830 in the US inventory.)
That depletion has global repercussions, most pressingly in Ukraine where top-end US interceptors are essential for shielding civilians from Russia’s most sophisticated ballistic missiles.
Trump’s attitude to that conflict has evolved from craven pro-Kremlin partisanship and an assumption of inevitable Russian victory to grudging respect for Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s fortitude and ingenuity in proving that assumption wrong. But the shift is not stable. It depends on undertakings by Nato’s European members to cover the cost of arming Kyiv.
If Trump had used normal diplomacy to cajole European democracies into financing the defence of their eastern flank, it would count as a foreign policy success – rebalancing the relationship to both sides’ benefit. But he did it with credulous admiration for Vladimir Putin and deranged demands for territory in Greenland. As a result, the European drive to autonomy looks less like burden-sharing and more like a hedge against American perfidy.
It isn’t just Europe where US allies feel burned. Gulf states that found themselves on the frontline of Iranian retaliation in a war they didn’t start or want, expected a more reliable umbrella of protection. They feel unrewarded for their decades of service, hosting US military bases and functioning as proxies for American interests in the region.
Last week Trump abruptly cut short a joint military exercise with South Korea – a loyal Asian partner to the US. A rational explanation, and the one preferred by Seoul, was that US forces were overstretched by their Middle Eastern entanglement. Trump framed it instead as an amicable gesture towards North Korean tyrant Kim Jong-un, whose regime he judged to be “unthreatening and respectful”.
Such civility, lavished on a monstrous dictatorship, is withheld from Canada, a benign democracy. Trump dismisses his northern neighbour as an economic freeloader, barely even a proper country; a mislabelled territory that should be the 51st US state.
Unsurprisingly, that attitude sours relations. Canadian prime minister Mark Carney pulled out of trade talks last weekend, citing unreasonable last-minute demands from US negotiators. Trump responded with punitive tariffs, to which the Canadians promise “dollar-for-dollar” retaliation.
The smaller economy is likely to suffer more from a trade war. But for Carney the cost in reduced commerce had to be weighed against the political damage he may incur if seen to capitulate to Trump’s bullying. He knows the US president takes concessions as an invitation to come back with yet more demands. He also knows that November’s midterm elections are likely to flip the House of Representatives to Democratic party control, and possibly the Senate too.
Trump cannot be chastened by unwelcome election results. He would rather deny their validity. But irrefutable evidence of failure at the ballot box may at least stir some Republicans out of stupefied obedience to a commander-in-chief whose way of governing has made their party less popular and left their country friendless.
Even if the constitutional mechanisms that are supposed to keep a president in check are only partly rehabilitated, the spell of impunity is broken. The cult of personality that once made Trump look like an irrepressible force of nature has shrunk to a sycophantic sect. An administration that styled itself as a national revolution looks more like a kleptocratic junta, using the privileges of office to pilfer what it can as the clock runs down.
The president still has followers across the country. A hard core bring unshakable devotion to the cause. But even some of them can surely sense the decay of purpose and whiff of panic in a man running out of ammunition.
Trump’s reign is far from over. With his hands on the levers of American power he can still do a lot of damage. But the rest of the world has learned to read his lurches, anticipate his spasms, manoeuvre around him. The phase of deference is past. Now is the time of planning for whatever comes next in the dimming light of a waning star.
- 
  Rafael Behr is a Guardian columnist

articles.title: What do we know about the Syria and Israel meeting in Jordan?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What do we know about the Syria and Israel meeting in Jordan, and efforts to revive negotiations?
The meeting that brought Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and Israeli Mossad chief Roman Gofman together in Jordan on Sunday, 23 August, raised questions about the possibility of reviving Syria-Israel negotiations after months of deadlock and rising tensions on the ground.
The meeting was mediated by the United States and hosted by Jordan, with the participation of security and military officials from both sides, according to Damascus, at a time when contacts between the two sides had stopped following the Israeli airstrike on Abu al-Duhur airbase in the Idlib countryside on 18 August.
The meeting, which brought the Syrian foreign minister together with the head of the Israeli foreign intelligence service, was the highest-level publicly announced direct contact since the start of the security track between the two sides.
Gofman held a phone call with al-Shaibani on 14 Aug. before tensions escalated and led to the bombing of Abu al-Duhur.
The far-right Netanyahu-led government claimed that the Israeli army had repeatedly recommended attacking the airport, located in the eastern Idlib countryside, based on intelligence that allegedly indicated Turkey intended to carry out activities inside the airport that would threaten "Israel's security".
Damascus says the meeting focused on de-escalation and halting Israeli attacks, arrests and targeting operations, as well as discussing the revival of Syria-Israel negotiations to reach a security agreement that could later form the basis for a more comprehensive agreement.
It also stressed that any arrangements must respect Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity and its right to rebuild its army and determine its alliances.
Al-Shaibani had said in an interview with Reuters on Saturday that Damascus expected security negotiations with Israel to resume soon, despite the lack of trust between the two sides.
He added that Syria's priority was to stop Israeli attacks, with the security agreement ultimately leading to an Israeli withdrawal from all Syrian territory seized after the fall of Bashar al-Assad's regime at the end of 2024.
The Syrian minister said Damascus was extending its hand for diplomacy, understanding and peace, but needed Israeli steps in return to build trust.
He said contacts had been cut off after the bombing of Abu al-Duhur but considered communication necessary with a party that Damascus views as a direct threat to its security.
Damascus says the proposed agreement discussed in earlier stages had come close to completion.
It included the establishment of security zones in southern Syria, including a buffer zone where the United Nations would be the only presence, as well as other areas where Syrian forces would be deployed to varying degrees.
But al-Shaibani accused Israel of failing to show the necessary willingness to implement what had been agreed, while stressing that his country would not abandon Turkey's support for rebuilding the Syrian army. This issue has become one of the main sources of tension between Israel and Turkey in Syria.
Syria-Israel negotiations: Five rounds without an agreement
Jordan announced on Monday, 24 August, that it had hosted a meeting on Sunday to discuss de-escalation between Syria and Israel.
The Jordan News Agency quoted an official source saying, "The meeting was held at the request of our brothers in Syria and discussed de-escalation and achieving calm after the Israeli bombing of Syrian territory last week."
"Jordan affirms the Kingdom's absolute support for the Syrian government in its efforts to protect its security, stability and territorial integrity," the source added. "We stress the need to immediately halt the brutal Israeli attacks on Syria, for Israel to withdraw from occupied Syrian territory and to respect the 1974 disengagement agreement."
Meanwhile, the Syrian state news agency SANA quoted a diplomatic source at the Syrian Foreign Ministry on Sunday, 23 August, as saying that the meeting came following the latest Israeli bombing of Syrian territory and escalating tensions in the south of the country.
Discussions focused on establishing practical mechanisms to halt Israeli attacks, arrests and targeting operations and reviving the negotiating track to reach a security agreement that could form the basis of a future, more comprehensive agreement.
According to the source, the Syrian side stressed during the meeting that Syria is a sovereign state with the full right to rebuild and develop its national army and to determine its alliances and partnerships in line with its national interests.
Syrian officials also reiterated "its firm position that the occupied Golan is Syrian territory", noting that "discussion of its final status and the path leading to that remains premature at the current stage and that the immediate priority is the withdrawal of Israeli forces to the lines that existed before 8 Dec. 2024 and the reactivation and full implementation of the 1974 disengagement agreement."
The discussions also addressed the importance of supporting stability in Syria and maintaining regional security, including efforts aimed at bringing Turkey's and Israel's positions closer together and ensuring that the existing tensions between the two countries do not spill over into Syrian territory.
According to the source, the meeting was mainly focused on taking practical steps to de-escalate while exploring ways to return to the negotiating track, with Syria stressing that any security arrangements must respect its sovereignty, territorial integrity and sovereign rights.
The negotiations between al-Shaibani and Gofman did not start from scratch.
The two sides had held five previous rounds of negotiations, the latest in Paris in January, which ended with an agreement to increase the frequency of meetings and take confidence-building measures, in addition to establishing a channel for exchanging intelligence.
But these understandings did not prevent Israel from continuing its attacks inside Syrian territory, prompting Damascus to say that Israel had not practically adhered to what had been agreed.
The latest developments reveal the extent of the gap between the two sides.
The Israeli airstrike on Abu al-Duhur airbase, which targeted runways and facilities at the base, was followed by another Israeli strike in southern Syria on 22 Aug.
Israel, meanwhile, claims that its operations are linked to security concerns and preventing potential threats to its forces.
In this context, Syrian-Israeli relations expert Khaled Khalil told The New Arab that the latest contact represents the highest point in the negotiating track so far.
He noted that Syria-Israel negotiations in earlier stages had been conducted through an Israeli political and diplomatic team led by former Strategic Affairs Minister Ron Dermer.
He considered the shift in communication to the level of the Mossad chief a reflection of the increased importance of the security issue but ruled out a rapid breakthrough because of the crisis of trust and the big differences in the two sides' views.
Withdrawal for 'security'
The first sticking point in Syria-Israel negotiations concerns the fate of the sites seized by Israel in southern Syria after the fall of the Assad regime.
Damascus is demanding the withdrawal of Israeli forces to the lines that existed before Dec. 8, 2024, and the reactivation and full implementation of the 1974 disengagement agreement.
It also maintains that the Golan is occupied Syrian territory but considers discussion of its final status premature at the current stage.
But Israel does not appear prepared simply to return to the situation that existed before the fall of the previous regime.
The information circulating indicates that Israel wants security arrangements broader than those stipulated in the 1974 agreement, including restrictions on the size, armament and deployment of Syrian forces in the south.
Here, a fundamental dilemma emerges: Damascus wants negotiations to serve as a gateway to restoring sovereignty and an Israeli withdrawal, while Tel Aviv wants the new security arrangements to provide a long-term guarantee against any threat from Syrian territory.
Thus, the core dispute is no longer only over the principle of withdrawal, but also over the line to which Israel will withdraw and which of the sites it seized on the ground it will retain.
Southern Syria under attack
Southern Syria represents the most complicated sticking point in Syria-Israel negotiations and any potential agreement between them.
Israel desire a largely "demilitarised" south, with restrictions on the deployment of heavy weapons, missiles and drones near the Golan.
It also seeks guarantees preventing the return of Iranian influence or the activity of groups linked to Lebanon's "Hezbollah" in the area, alongside more effective mechanisms for monitoring the border.
On the other hand, Damascus rejects any formula that undermines its sovereign right to build its army and develop its capabilities. It explicitly said during the Jordan meeting that Syria is a sovereign state and has the right to rebuild and develop its army and determine its alliances and partnerships in line with its national interests.
Thus, negotiations over the south will not be merely technical but will concern the very concept of sovereignty: to what extent can Syria deploy its military within its own territory, and to what extent will Israel retain what it calls the right to intervene if it considers there to be a "threat" to its security?
There was no discussion regarding Israel's military capabilities, including its nuclear arsenal.
Turkey: The third party
The Turkish factor has emerged in recent weeks as one of the most sensitive issues in Israeli calculations.
Israel says any Turkish military deployment or the establishment of Turkish air defence infrastructure inside Syria could pose a threat to it, particularly because it could limit the freedom of action of the Israeli air force in Syrian and regional airspace.
The Mossad chief discussed Israeli concerns over the growing Turkish military presence in Syria with al-Shaibani during the phone call on 14 August, days before the bombing of Abu al-Duhur.
Damascus and Ankara deny plans to establish a Turkish base that threatens Israel, while US special envoy to Syria Tom Barrack recently described the Israeli strike as unnecessary escalation and pushed for a mechanism to prevent friction between Israel, Turkey and Syria.
Thus, Syria-Israel negotiations could become part of a broader regional negotiating track, involving not only relations between Damascus and Tel Aviv but also the future of Turkey's role in Syria.
Political analyst Ahmad al-Mousa remarked to TNA that Damascus took part in the Jordan meeting with clear sovereign demands, most notably an end to airstrikes and attacks, an Israeli withdrawal from the territories seized after the fall of the previous regime, a reduction in Israeli-Turkish tensions, and preservation of Syria's right to build its capabilities and establish its alliances.
Al-Mousa considers the negotiations at this stage not to represent normalisation, but rather security communication to manage the conflict and prevent a slide into open confrontation.
Political analyst Ghazi Dahman, meanwhile, believes that Israeli policy towards Syria has gone beyond the concept of security and defensive measures to an attempt to impose a long-term reality on the Syrian state.
He told TNA that continued strikes and incursions aim to keep Damascus weak and unstable.
Regardless of the differing assessments, the continuation of Israeli military operations alongside Syria-Israel negotiations represents one of the biggest problems facing the current track and leaves each round of negotiations vulnerable to collapse at the first escalation on the ground.
Little chance of sixth round succeeding
If Syria-Israel negotiations resume soon, the next round will face a more difficult test than previous rounds because the two sides will enter it with a record of mistrust and new realities on the ground.
In this context, Khaled Khalil believes that Israeli intransigence, along with domestic political considerations in Israel, makes rapid progress in Syria-Israel negotiations unlikely.
He believes the Israeli government may resort to escalation when facing political or regional pressure.
For its part, Damascus faces a different equation.
It wants to assert its sovereignty and recover the territories it lost control of, but at the same time it does not currently have the military capability to impose its conditions by force.
Therefore, negotiations appear to Damascus to be a tool for managing a transitional phase rather than a ready path to comprehensive peace.
Damascus says the security agreement could serve as a prelude to a broader agreement, but this possibility appears remote in the near term.
Even if the two sides succeed in agreeing on an end to attacks, a withdrawal and arrangements for the south, the ongoing Israeli occupation of Golan will remain postponed, along with questions of normalisation, diplomatic relations and the future of the borders.
Damascus maintains that the Golan is occupied Syrian territory while currently prioritising an end to attacks, an Israeli withdrawal from the recently occupied territories and the reactivation of the 1974 agreement.
At the same time, Israel is focused on security guarantees concerning southern Syria, limiting Turkey's military role and maintaining its freedom of action in Syrian airspace.
For this reason, a resumption of negotiations, if it happens, will not necessarily mean that a final agreement is near.
The next phase is more likely to begin with an attempt to establish a limited security understanding to prevent escalation before moving to more complicated political issues.
The key question remains: Can Washington turn the current de-escalation into an agreement that can be implemented, or will the negotiations remain hostage to changing military and political realities?
Article translated from Arabic by Afrah Almatwari. To read the original, click here.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Zelensky confirms UK, France approve producing SCALP/Storm Shadow missiles in Ukraine
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Zelensky confirms UK, France approve producing SCALP/Storm Shadow missiles in Ukraine
Key developments on Aug. 25:
- UK, France approve Storm Shadow/SCALP missile production in Ukraine, Zelensky says
- US asked Ukraine to refrain from striking Moscow during CIA chief's visit, source says
- Kellogg backs mobilizing Ukrainian women, parliament says it is not under consideration
- Kremlin dismisses Donbas free economic zone proposal
- Russian drone strikes border crossing between Ukraine, Moldova
- Ukrainian strike damages MiG-29 fighter jet at Russian air base
- 'Fabricated stories' — Kremlin accuses Ukraine of spreading false mobilization claims
Ukraine has received approval from the U.K. and France to produce long-range Storm Shadow/SCALP missiles, President Volodymyr Zelensky said during a press conference with Estonian President Alar Karis in Kyiv on Aug. 25.
Zelensky said French President Emmanuel Macron had confirmed that restrictions on the SCALP missiles and related licenses would be lifted.
"We will act. I believe this is a strong positive and a strong decision," Zelensky added in a post on Telegram.
The announcementcame as Zelensky and Karis met in Kyiv. The Estonian president arrived in Ukraine to mark Independence Day on Aug. 24 and discuss military support, air defense, and broader cooperation.
The decision helps Ukraine move closer to producing the missiles at home. The U.K. has agreed to let European defense company MBDA share classified technical information on British-made parts of SCALP missiles with Ukraine, the U.K. government said on Aug. 24.
The SCALP is a long-range cruise missile built jointly by France and the U.K., which calls it the Storm Shadow. It has a range of up to 250 kilometers (155 miles) and is designed for precision strikes on fixed targets, including at night and in bad weather.
Norway has also confirmed $9 billion in financial support outside the EU framework for Ukraine in 2027, Zelensky said, adding that Oslo wants to help finance the Freyja project.
Ukraine also received confirmation that it will receive several Crotale air defense systems and their VT-1 missiles, as well as AIM missiles and additional missiles for Patriot systems, Zelensky said. The president did not specify which country will provide this assistance.
read also
US asked Ukraine to refrain from striking Moscow during CIA chief's visit, source says
The U.S. asked Ukraine not to strike Moscow and St. Petersburg while CIA Director John Ratcliffe is visiting Russia, a person familiar with the situation told the Kyiv Independent on Aug. 25.
"They don't believe in the strength of (Russian President Vladimir) Putin's air defenses," they said, adding that Kyiv agreed to pause strikes against the cities between Aug. 24 and 26.
A U.S. official confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that Ratcliffe is scheduled to meet senior Russian officials, but it remains unclear what is on the agenda. The Kremlin has not officially commented on the visit.
This marks Ratcliffe's first known official trip to Russia. The CIA director has nevertheless maintained contact with his Russian counterpart, SVR chief Sergei Naryshkin, who has previously signaled readiness to meet the U.S. spy chief.
The Ukrainian side was told that a U.S. delegation would travel to Russia, but was not initially informed that Ratcliffe would be a part of it, a source told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukrainian officials are expected to receive a debrief after the trip, though it is unclear whether the CIA director will travel to Kyiv in person, they said.
read also
Kellogg backs mobilizing Ukrainian women, parliament says it is not under consideration
Former U.S. Special Envoy for Ukraine Keith Kellogg said he supports mobilizing Ukrainian women into the military, while Parliament's National Security Committee stressed on Aug. 25 that no such measure is being prepared or considered.
"So do I believe women should be mobilized into the army? My answer is yes, because they fight no worse than men," Kellogg said in an interviewwith the Naspravdi MAX YouTube channel published on Aug. 24.
Kellogg added that it is "very important for women, as part of society, to serve," saying he saw no problem with the idea "personally or professionally."
Hours after Kellogg's remarks drew attention in Ukraine, the committee issued an official statement saying that the mobilization of women "is not being carried out, prepared, or considered."
The committee said there were no legislative initiatives, draft laws, or internal discussions on mobilizing women and stressed that women currently join Ukraine's Defense Forces exclusively on a voluntary basis.
"Statements by individual speakers who publicly speculate on this topic do not reflect actual legislative work or the position of the committee," the statement read.
read also
Kremlin dismisses Donbas free economic zone proposal
The Kremlin on Aug. 25 shot down a U.S.-backed proposal to establish a free economic zone in Ukraine's Donbas as part of a potential peace deal, alleging the region belongs to Russia.
"It is unlikely that any third party could administer Russia's regions," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told journalists.
Russia views the partially occupied Donbas — an eastern Ukrainian region comprised of the Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts — as its territory and has incorporated this claim into its constitution.
Moscow's demand that Kyiv cede the areas still under Ukrainian control has become a key sticking point in peace talks, as Ukraine continues to call for a ceasefire along the current front lines.
Peskov's comments come after President Volodymyr Zelensky said that a one-page peace plan drafted by Ukraine, the U.S., and European partners included Washington's proposal for a buffer zone in Donbas.
"In other words, we and the Russians both take equal steps back, creating a buffer called a free economic zone under some kind of administration," Zelensky told journalists during a press briefing over the weekend.
"It is still unclear whose administration, but it would be some kind of third party."
The peace proposal also included a ceasefire and outlined the roles NATO and the EU would play in the effort, Zelensky said, without providing further details.
read also
Russian drone strikes border crossing between Ukraine, Moldova
A Russian Shahed-type drone strike overnight on Aug. 25 damaged the Vynohradivka border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova in Odesa Oblast, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
In a post on X, Sybiha called on the international community to "condemn Russia’s systematic targeting of civilian transport corridors and critical border infrastructure."
The State Border Guard Service reported that the passage of citizens and vehicles through the checkpoint was suspended. Transport was being redirected to other checkpoints.
This is the third attack on a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova in the last two weeks. Sybiha called this "a clear pattern," accusing Russia of "deliberately trying to disrupt connectivity" between Ukraine and its neighbor.
Ukrainian strike damages MiG-29 fighter jet at Russian air base
Ukrainian strikes on Millerovo airbase in Russia's Rostov Oblast damaged a Mig-29 fighter jet on Aug. 24, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed on Aug. 25.
The Mig-29 is a fourth generation fighter jet designed in the Soviet Union, meant to establish air superiority and provide frontline air defense. Both Ukrainian and Russian forces use the fighter jet in their air forces.
Ukrainian forces also struck a specialized Peresvet-M electronic warfare system in Luhansk Oblast, a radio-electronic station meant to surpress Starlink communication in Mirne in occupied Crimea, and a Russian military warehouse in Primorsk, Zaporizhzhia Oblast, the statement read.
read also
'Fabricated stories' — Kremlin accuses Ukraine of spreading false mobilization claims
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov accused Ukrainian authorities of trying to "ideologically destabilize the situation" in Russia by spreading reports about a possible new Russian mobilization, in an interview with Russian media outlet RTVI on Aug. 25.
Peskov was responding to questions about the Kremlin's view on another Russian mobilization announcement and whether such a scenario is being considered.
"All of this is being planted by the Ukrainian authorities," Peskov said, adding that "these are all fabricated stories that are deliberately being planted in the information space."
Speculation about another Russian mobilization has intensified in recent months as Russia’s battlefield gains slow and its voluntary recruitment system struggles to compensate for mounting losses.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 23 that Russia plans to mobilize around 300,000 people after State Duma elections in September, largely avoiding major cities to limit public backlash. He described the plan as "peripheral mobilization."
Russia has repeatedly denied plans for mobilization, both now and in 2022. On Sept. 13, 2022, Peskov said that neither full nor partial mobilization was "on the agenda." Eight days later, Putin announced a partial mobilization, calling up around 300,000 reservists.

articles.title: CIA Director John Ratcliffe Visits Moscow, US Media Reports
articles.body:
CIA Director John Ratcliffe reportedly visited Moscow on Tuesday, Aug. 25, for private meetings with Russian authorities, in his first known visit to the country since taking charge of the agency.
CBS News reported the visit on Tuesday, citing sources familiar with the matter after a US Air Force Boeing C-17 Globemaster III military transport plane landed at Moscow’s Vnukovo Airport. The plane flew in from Riga, Latvia, raising questions about the flight’s unusual route.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Neither Washington nor Moscow commented on the purpose of the visit or publicly identified the US official that arrived in Russia, according to CBS News.
“We have no information about this,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said when asked about the aircraft, adding that Russia was not planning meetings with the US administration this week.
Axios, citing two anonymous US officials, reported that Washington had informed Kyiv ahead of the alleged visit that a high-level US delegation was traveling to Moscow and had asked Ukraine to refrain from strikes on the Russian capital.
Sources in Ukrainian government circles later confirmed the account to Suspilne media, saying the request also covered St. Petersburg.
Neither the White House nor the Kremlin had confirmed Ratcliffe’s reported visit at the time of publication.
Visit comes amid stalled peace efforts
Ratcliffe’s alleged visit comes as US-mediated efforts to advance peace negotiations between Russia and Ukraine remain stalled.
Ukraine Receives Additional Patriot Missiles, Zelensky Says
Moscow continues to dismiss the prospect of a ceasefire and has yet to join the negotiating table, which Ukraine is seeking to encourage by targeting Russia’s critical oil and energy infrastructure, alongside the logistics network.
According to CBS News, the CIA director has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts, though it has not been confirmed whether Russian authorities had been informed of his visit in advance.
CIA role in previous detainee exchanges
The agency has also been involved in recent detainee exchanges between the US and Russia, CBS News reported.
In April 2025, US-Russian dual national Ksenia Karelina was released in an exchange after Ratcliffe had personally negotiated her case.
The CIA was also reportedly involved in a 2024 prisoner exchange that secured the release of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich and former US Marine Paul Whelan.
Former CIA Director William Burns traveled to Moscow in November 2021, meeting with Russian officials and speaking directly with Russian President Vladimir Putin to deliver a warning from Washington against a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to CBS News.
C-17 flight draws attention
The US aircraft – identified as RCH4555 – departed Riga at around 8:50 a.m. before landing in Vnukovo airport at roughly 10:04 a.m.
Flight-tracking data indicated that the aircraft first arrived in Riga on Sunday, Aug. 23, after departing from Camp Springs, Maryland, home to Andrews Air Force Base.
The C-17 Globemaster III is a military transport aircraft designed to carry personnel, military equipment and heavy cargo over long distances, including armored vehicles and helicopters.
Kyiv secures new defense commitments
The alleged visit came as Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day on Monday, Aug. 24, with allies gathering in Kyiv to pledge additional support and air defenses.
On the same day, Ukraine signed an artificial-intelligence (AI) defense partnership with the UK, granting British researchers access to Ukraine’s Avengers AI Labs battlefield-data platform to support the joint development of new military technologies.
The agreement marked another step in the countries’ defense partnership.
On Tuesday, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Ukraine has received additional Patriot missiles critically needed for intercepting Russian ballistic missiles. He also said that Ukraine had received confirmation from the UK regarding the production of SCALP long-range missiles.
Meanwhile, the US has refused to join a UN statement condemning Russia’s strikes on Ukraine again as 50 countries called for an immediate ceasefire.
The US has previously declined to support similar Ukrainian initiatives at the UN.
US President Donald Trump has long resisted calling Russia as the aggressor in Ukraine’s war, although his diplomatic stance changed in the past months due to Ukraine’s battlefield advance.
During the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey on July 7-8, Trump has even floated granting Ukraine a license to produce its own Patriot interceptors, though he has since softened his earlier commitment.
