articles.title: Former US spy chief Gabbard warned Trump killing Khamenei could empower radical regime - WSJ
articles.body:
Before attacking Iran, US President Donald Trump was warned by US intelligence that killing Iran's former supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, could result in him being replaced by a more radical regime with greater interest in acquiring nuclear weapons, according to a report from The Wall Street Journal on Tuesday.
In the lead-up to the February attack that started the US-Israel war with Iran, Trump reportedly called his intelligence chief at that time, Tulsi Gabbard, to the Oval Office to discuss the advisability of a full-scale military assault.
According to sources familiar with the meeting who spoke to WSJ, Gabbard cautioned Trump that killing Iran’s supreme leader could bring about a hard-line government that would be more inclined to pursue nuclear arms.
She also warned that Iran might swiftly close the Strait of Hormuz, jeopardizing the global energy market. Additionally, she argued that targeting Iran could lead to attacks on US forces and allies in the Middle East, which would raise questions about American reliability and resolve among its partners.
Security officials advise against launching an attack
Several of Trump’s senior national security officials similarly advised against launching an attack, expressing concerns about potential mass casualties, a limited weapons stockpile, and readiness issues for an overstretched military.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Joint Chiefs Chairman Gen. Dan Caine, and Adm. Brad Cooper, the head of US Central Command, reportedly briefed Trump several times on plans to strike Iranian targets with the expressed goal of ultimately weakening the Islamic Republic and incapacitating its military forces while allowing Israel to focus on targeting Iran's top leadership.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also reportedly informed Trump that the potential attack would provide him with a rare opportunity to dismantle Iran’s nuclear program and enhance his legacy as a peacemaker, WSJ noted.
Hegseth and Caine allegedly repeatedly claimed that they could manage any complications that might arise during the operation, according to officials who attended the meetings.
Despite receiving warnings from Gabbard and other senior national security officials during this timeframe, Trump ultimately dismissed their concerns. Instead, he echoed Hegseth and Caine’s confidence, suggesting the military could address any issues as they arose.
Vance pushed for negotiations with Iran before Op. Epic Fury
Another voice of caution came from Vice President JD Vance.
US officials told WSJ that Vance advocated for a more cautious approach during meetings leading up to Operation Epic Fury.
He reportedly suggested that Iran might be swayed to dismantle its nuclear program through negotiations. Vance pointed out that while pursuing a deal carried some risk, it would be less costly than the potential consequences of war.
He emphasized that Iran’s economy was already suffering due to heavy US sanctions. If negotiations failed, he argued, Trump would then have greater legitimacy to execute a swift and overwhelming military operation against Iran.
Although Trump reportedly considered Vance’s perspective, US officials told WSJ that he was ultimately persuaded by Pentagon presentations outlining more “decisive” options.
Tensions with Iran unresolved after six months of war
Six months after the attack that kicked off the war, military clashes between Iran and the US have paused, but disagreements over the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s nuclear assets, and US sanctions have persisted.
Trump’s latest statement regarding the war came on Tuesday as he claimed that the US is closely watching the strait and nuclear sites from space.
In a post on Truth Social, he also asserted that all mines placed by Iran have been removed from Hormuz and that any attempt by Tehran to place new ones would be stopped.
Meanwhile, Iran has made its own demands regarding the state clear by sending messages to Washington through Pakistani mediators as recently as Tuesday.

articles.title: New US sanctions put pressure on Iran as petrol queues form
articles.body:
Washington has turned to pulling economic levers six months into a war on Iran that has ground to a stalemate militarily, with peace talks stalled and most traffic through the crucial Strait of Hormuz blocked.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday laid out plans for the "economic asphyxiation" of Iran, saying the "objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime".
Announcing the new sanctions, Bessent said countries that did not support the US economic campaign would "share in the isolation" of Iran, adding Trump was making phone calls to world leaders asking that they halt interactions with Tehran.
The Treasury Department said expanded secondary sanctions would target Iran's digital assets and its technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors.
It also issued new sanctions against 60 individuals, companies and vessels that allegedly aid Iran in oil revenue generation, weapons procurement and cyber operations.
Iran, however, was dismissive of the threat and predicted "another defeat" for Washington.
"We've been waiting for these plans for a long time, and the government is and was ready and has a two-year plan to manage these events," said Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh.
From Washington’s new sanctions against Iran and Tehran’s warnings over the Strait of Hormuz to fresh diplomatic efforts involving Oman, tensions across the region remain high.
Follow The New Arab for the latest developments.
Rubio says US not expected to launch new Iran strikes: Axios
Secretary of State Marco Rubio has told several foreign ministers from allied countries in recent days that "for time being" the United States is not expected to launch new strikes against Iran, and will instead focus on other means of pressure, Axios reported on Tuesday, citing a US official and a second source with knowledge of the matter.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio [GETTY]
US-led Gaza peace board warns Hamas against flying kites
The US-led board supervising a Gaza peace plan on Tuesday warned Hamas against flying kites, after Israel threatened retaliatory strikes.
"All militant activity in Gaza must stop, including the flying of kites. We have conveyed this message directly through the established mechanism," an official on President Donald Trump's "Board of Peace" said on condition of anonymity.
"Israel, too, must comply with the ceasefire. Military action cannot extend beyond responding to genuine and imminent threats," the official said.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday warned Hamas that Israel would step up operations in Gaza if it launches kites, drones or balloons.
The threat came after a series of kites reportedly were found across the Gaza border in southern Israel, communities traumatised by the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023.
The episode revived memories of incendiary kites and balloons once launched from Gaza. The latest kites are not known to have had any explosives, although Israeli media reported at least one with a political message.
Hamas political bureau member Basem Naim voiced outrage at the warning on kites conveyed via the Board of Peace.
"What audacity! Is it conceivable that attempts to appease the war criminal Netanyahu have led them to describe innocent children's activities as armed activities, while Netanyahu continues to kill and destroy daily despite the agreement?"
The United Nations earlier Tuesday described the Israeli threats over the kites as unacceptable.
"On the threat of expulsion due to children's kite flying, I hope we can all agree that this is outrageous," UN rights office spokeswoman Ravina Shamdasani told reporters in Geneva.
Trump maintains Israel condition for Saudi nuclear deal
US President Donald Trump has sent to Congress an agreement on civil nuclear energy with Saudi Arabia, and the president maintains his position that the pact will only move forward if the kingdom joins the Abraham Accords, a US administration official told Reuters on Tuesday.
Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs, Kazem Gharibabadi, told Iranian television that Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz “has put great pressure on the American side”, adding that developments on Tuesday were largely in line with demands Tehran had made before negotiations.
Gharibabadi said the current developments could be interpreted as a “retreat” by the US administration from its previous positions.
Explaining the details of the Iranian-Omani understanding on the Strait of Hormuz, he stressed that the agreement did not mean the strait would reopen immediately, saying the two issues were separate.
Gharibabadi said ships had travelled through Omani waters for the past 58 years, causing “serious damage to Iran”. He added that the Strait of Hormuz had now become an issue of Iranian national security, requiring fundamental changes to maritime entry and exit routes.
Under the understanding, vessels entering the Gulf would travel through Iranian waters, while those leaving would use Omani territorial waters, with ships on both routes passing through Iranian waters.
The deputy foreign minister described the arrangement as being “like a highway back and forth”, with a total width of around seven miles.
He said the route was temporary and that Iran and Oman would need to negotiate a new permanent route within 30 to 60 days to replace the previous maritime traffic arrangement.
US envoy hails dissolution of Kurdish-led force in Syria
The United States on Tuesday hailed the dissolution of a Kurdish-led, Washington-backed force in Syria that was at the forefront of the battle against the Islamic State group, and its merger into the country's army.
"This is what real integration looks like: not winners and losers, but former counterparts with differing points of view crafting a diplomatic solution to strengthen the sovereign nation of Syria. One army, one government, one state," said the US special envoy to Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack, who is also the ambassador to Turkey.
Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank on Tuesday attacked journalists from news agency AFP reporting on tension with Palestinians, in violence that left at least five people injured, the reporters and medics said.
A three-person team from the international news agency had travelled to the village of Jannatah near Bethlehem to report on Israeli activists who conduct solidarity visits to support Palestinians facing harassment by Israeli settlers, who recently blocked a road in the area.
After an altercation broke out between the settlers and activists, the Israeli military ordered journalists to leave what it called a "closed military zone", at which point two additional cars full of settlers swooped in.
The settlers, many of them children, threw stones towards the journalists and activists. According to AFP, one journalist ducked a stone but then a child settler struck him in the chin with a stick, causing minor bleeding, he said.
AFP added that the journalists returned to see their two parked cars both damaged, with back windshields smashed in and tyres punctured. Activists' cars suffered similar damage.
Five people were treated for injuries, the Palestine Red Crescent Society said, with AFP journalists reporting seeing at least one Israeli activist taken in a Palestinian ambulance.
During the clash an Israeli soldier temporarily seized the camera of a video journalist but handed it back afterward, the AFP journalists reported.
An Israeli military spokesperson said that the temporary confiscation of the camera "is currently being reviewed".
Israeli police joined the military to collect evidence on the damage to cars and "a police investigation has been opened into the incident", the military spokesperson said.
More than 500,000 Israelis live in the West Bank, which Israel has occupied since 1967, home to around three million Palestinians, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing government advancing more construction ahead of October 27 elections.
Violence against Palestinians by Israeli settlers has increased dramatically since the October 7, 2023 attack on Israel by Hamas from the Gaza Strip.
Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs, Kazem Gharibabadi, has warned that US mine-detection vessels would become “very good targets” for Iran if they entered the region.
He said US President Donald Trump’s statements on demining were “only aimed at calming the markets”.
Gharibabadi said Tehran’s response to US sanctions would shift towards targeting what he described as the economic interests of its adversaries, rather than responding to the measures through previous methods.
He also questioned why Iran should wait for the United States to launch an attack, raising the possibility that Tehran could take pre-emptive action.
Gharibabadi said Iran would unveil new capabilities if US measures continued.
He added that the Strait of Hormuz was not Iran’s only means of responding to the United States, warning that Washington should not assume it was the only side capable of causing economic damage.
Britain backs US efforts for diplomatic solution on Iran
British Finance Minister John Healey said on Tuesday that the country supports U.S. efforts to secure a diplomatic solution on Iran and welcomed steps to increase pressure, including the expanded sanctions on Iran announced Monday.
Healey also called on Iran to cease its "de-stabilising activity" across the region, including in the Strait of Hormuz.
Israel expels Dutch officials over ‘anti-Israel moves’
Israel’s Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar has announced the immediate expulsion of Dutch representatives from the International Support Center for Gaza in Israel, citing what he described as “a series of anti-Israel moves by the Dutch government”.
“I decided so today, with the approval of Prime Minister Netanyahu,” Sa’ar said, pointing to a Dutch law banning trade in Israeli products from the occupied West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, which is set to come into force next month.
Sa’ar said the Dutch embassy in Israel and US officials were notified on Sunday evening, with the representatives given one week to leave the country.
He claimed the Dutch government’s policies had been “accompanied by an unprecedented wave of antisemitism and boycotts” in the Netherlands.
“Whoever acts against Israel will have no foothold in the region,” he said. “Israel will not allow steps against it without a response.”
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei has criticised the latest US sanctions against Iran- referred to as “Economic D-Day”.
“Those who prefer to appear ‘as obedient as shadows’ say: ‘This is fine.’ But hold on. It is absolutely not fine," he wrote in a post on X.
“When a bully declares that every bank, company, port, and government must choose between obeying Washington’s whims or facing American vengeance, this is no longer just about Iran.”
Syria's SDF dissolves as part of integration with Damascus
The Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces has been dissolved, the armed militant group's leader said on Tuesday, a major step in the integration plan agreed on earlier this year with the Islamist-led government in Damascus.
"We announce today the end of the mission of the Syrian Democratic Forces and announce with full responsibility its dissolution as an independent military force," SDF commander Mazloum Abdi said in a televised speech.
The government and the group, which helped defeat the Islamic State with U.S. backing and held parts of northern and eastern Syria, agreed in January to a phased integration of Kurdish fighters into the state, a plan Washington called a "historic milestone".
The deal came shortly after government forces under President Ahmed al-Sharaa launched a lightning offensive in January, taking swathes of the areas the SDF held.
Abdi said that the announcement followed an agreement with Sharaa after the integration of the group's forces into the army.
The Kurdish People's Protection Units, which formed the core of the SDF, had already been integrated within state forces with its commander, Sipan Hamo, appointed in March deputy defence minister for the country's eastern territories.
The SDF dissolution comes as the new leaders in Damascus seek to resolve internal strife and rebuild Syria, with support from Washington, after nearly 14 years of civil war and decades of isolation under former President Bashar al-Assad's rule.
US Secret Service aware of Iran threat against Barron Trump
The US Secret Service is aware of a video broadcast by Iranian state television discussing a potential plot to assassinate U.S. President Donald Trump's youngest son, a spokesperson said on Tuesday.
"The US Secret Service is aware of the video and investigates anything that can be perceived as a threat toward our protectees. Out of concern for operational security, we do not discuss matters of protective intelligence," Secret Service spokesperson Nate Herring said in an email.
A three-minute video broadcast by Iranian state TV discussed a potential plot to assassinate Barron Trump, 20, claiming that he was being monitored and alleging that a $10 million bounty had been offered for his killing.
The United States and Iran have kept up hostile rhetoric during a nearly six-month-old war started by the U.S. and Israel in February. Reuters reported earlier this month that the U.S. has received several warnings from Israel over the past year that Iran intended to assassinate  Trump, according to officials, including before a secret Air Force One ruse in Turkey.
Trump has described himself as "number one on the kill list for Iran."
Barron Trump and his mother First Lady Melania Trump [Getty]
Oman FM says to announce temporary Hormuz shipping corridor
Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said on Tuesday that he hoped his country and Iran would soon announce the establishment of a temporary shipping corridor in the Strait of Hormuz after weeks of negotiations.
"I am hopeful that we will soon announce a temporary corridor for the Strait of Hormuz, as well as practical arrangements to restore safe navigation. Future management of the strait and a permanent solution will follow in due course," Albusaidi said in a statement after meeting Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Tehran.
UN chief 'greatly alarmed', Israeli forces enter UNRWA base
United Nations chief Antonio Guterres on Tuesday condemned an incursion by Israeli forces on a training center run by the UN agency for Palestinian refugees (UNRWA) in an east Jerusalem suburb.
"The Secretary-General is greatly alarmed at this development, as it will deprive young people of the vocational education they were receiving," spokesman Stephane Dujarric said.
He added that the training center "and other UNRWA premises are premises of the United Nations. They are inviolable and immune from any form of interference."
Oman's top diplomat held talks in Iran on Tuesday, Tehran said, as the two countries seek a way to regulate transit through the Strait of Hormuz, which has emerged as a flashpoint in the Middle East war.
"Oman's Foreign Minister Badr al-Busaidi met and talked with Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in Tehran," an Iranian foreign ministry statement said.
No further details of the meeting were immediately announced.
Katz vows to keep Israeli troops in Syria during visit
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz made a rare visit to troops in southern Syria on Tuesday, reiterating a pledge to keep forces in the area as long as there were "threats" to his country's security.
The visit comes a week after Israel bombed the disused Abu Duhur base in northwestern Syria, claiming it wanted to prevent Turkish troops deploying to the facility. Ankara has denied any visit to the site.
In southern Syria, Israeli forces have been stationed in a "security zone" since the fall of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.
They occupy what was previously a buffer zone patrolled by the United Nations that had separated Israeli and Syrian forces in the Israeli-occupied Golan since 1974.
"There is daily activity here to thwart threats, to eliminate remnants of the old regime, to prevent dangerous consolidation of the new regime," Katz said according to a video statement from his office.
"The message is clear to the president of Syria as well: when you wake up in the morning in your palace in Damascus, look up at Mount Hermon and see the [Israeli forces]-- you know we are here to protect our communities and our border," he added.
"As long as there are threats, the [Israeli forces] will remain here to guarantee our security -- this is what we have done and this is what we intend to continue doing in the future," Katz said.
Israel has carried out hundreds of strikes in Syria since the fall of Assad and made repeated incursions into Syrian territory.
Trump says executions of Iran protesters must stop
US President Donald Trump expressed outrage on Tuesday at the mounting number of executions in Iran of people allegedly involved in mass protests earlier this year before the Middle East war began.
"The failing Islamic Republic of Iran is not paying large segments of their military, while at the same time killing protesters, even when they are not protesting, at levels not seen before," he wrote on Truth Social.
"It is a humanitarian crisis of epic proportions, and must be stopped, NOW," he added.
It was not immediately clear what new information had spurred the early morning post, but there has been a steady increase in executions since the outbreak of the war on February 28.
The joint US-Israeli strikes which kicked off the war came weeks after the violent quelling of mass protests in Iran.
Rallies initially began in late December over outrage at the high cost of living, but rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on January 8 and 9.
Iranian authorities reported more than 3,000 deaths, but attributed the violence to "terrorist acts" orchestrated by the United States and Israel.
Rights groups based abroad recorded a far higher toll and said the security forces had fired on demonstrators.
Airlines have largely resumed services through parts of the Gulf, but some destinations remain disrupted.
Dubai continues to be one of the most affected destinations, with several European and Asian carriers extending suspensions into October or later.
Multiple Lufthansa Group airlines maintain suspensions to destinations including Dubai and Beirut through late October.
British Airways, Air Canada, Singapore Airlines and Wizz Air have also extended suspensions on a range of Middle East routes. Air France is meanwhile moving towards resumption of its Middle East destinations.
Airlines moving toward resumption
Air France: Beirut flights are suspended until September 1, flights to Riyadh and Dubai suspended until August 25.
Oil down as traders weigh US sanctions threat against Iran
Oil prices slipped for a second day on Tuesday as traders judged the latest US warning of sanctions against Iran to have reduced the risk of renewed military strikes, after six months of war in the Gulf.
The measures appeared softer than analysts had expected, and were accompanied by news of further shuttle diplomacy as a key Pakistani mediator met with the Iranian president on Monday.
The news helped calm oil markets, with prices falling around three percent and the international benchmark Brent back below $90 a barrel.
The main US exchanges rose in early trading, matching earlier gains in Europe, though London slipped back into the red in the afternoon.
Talks to reopen the Strait of Hormuz have remained stalled for weeks, which had pushed oil prices up for most of August -- fuelling inflation fears and unnerving bond investors.
The US said expanded "secondary" sanctions would target Iran's digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors -- but gave no timeline and named no specific countries beyond Iran.
Long queues have formed at petrol stations across Tehran as motorists rush to refuel amid growing concerns over fuel supplies and the impact of Washington’s latest sanctions on Iran.
The developments come as the US intensifies economic pressure on Tehran, while Iranian officials insist the country is prepared to withstand the measures.
Follow our live coverage for the latest updates from Iran, the US and the wider region.

articles.title: What Trump's 'economic D-Day' on Iran means for the Gulf
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
What Trump's 'economic D-Day' on Iran means for the Gulf
The Trump administration is aggressively attempting to cut off Iran’s financial lifelines.
On 24 August, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced “Operation Economic Outcast,” a sweeping sanctions campaign designed to isolate Tehran and pressure its government toward collapse.
The United States says it has identified the networks, companies, vessels, and financial channels helping Iran sell oil, obtain technology, and generate revenue, while warning countries and businesses that continue working with Tehran that they could face secondary sanctions.
The new measures target more than 60 individuals, companies, and vessels connected to Iran’s oil trade, nuclear and missile programs, cyber operations, and financial networks.
The campaign also focuses on Iran’s international partners, with possible secondary sanctions affecting sectors such as shipping, aviation, technology, gold, and digital assets.
China is particularly important because it purchases approximately 90 percent of Iran’s exported oil, yet Bessent stopped short of announcing specific penalties against Chinese banks or businesses.
The Trump administration’s escalating pressure on Iran will inevitably impose heavy human and economic costs on its population.
Iran was already grappling with severe inflation, a collapsing currency, unemployment, power shortages, and rising prices before “Operation Economic Outcast”.
The new measures will only deepen these hardships for ordinary citizens. But whether inflicting greater pain on Iranians will translate into a US victory with the Trump administration achieving its objectives is another question. There is good reason to doubt that this strategy will succeed.
It is clear that the Trump administration is frustrated with the course of the war over the past six months. The White House now appears determined to pursue its goals through a new strategy that carries far lower political costs at home, where the war has long been unpopular and is becoming increasingly so.
“Trump is turning back to economic pressure on Iran because military force failed to deliver the victory he expected,” said Negar Mortazavi, a Washington-based journalist, host of The Iran Podcast, and senior fellow at the Center for International Policy, in an interview with The New Arab.
At this point, the success of “Operation Economic Outcast” is anything but guaranteed, particularly given Iran’s decades-long experience of circumventing American and European sanctions, while the strategy will also require Washington to balance its goal of isolating Tehran with the economic and geopolitical risks associated with confronting China and other major trading partners.
Although the administration’s sanctions strategy is strikingly belligerent, it is also fundamentally vague, with no clear answer as to what comes next, particularly given its admission that fully enforcing the measures could destabilise the global financial system, as the former American diplomat Robert Malley noted.
While the “D-Day sanctions” will inflict greater economic pain and human suffering on Iranians, they may also push the Islamic Republic toward a more aggressive posture, increasing the likelihood of military escalation if Iranian officials conclude that the White House’s ultimate goal is regime change.
The paradox is that the Trump administration is pursuing economic pressure precisely to achieve its objectives without returning to war, at least until after this year’s US midterm elections.
The UAE is key to Trump's pressure campaign
The United Arab Emirates (UAE), and particularly Dubai, is central to this effort because of its longstanding role as an important Iranian commercial, financial, and re-export gateway.
Shortly before the Trump administration unveiled “Operation Economic Outcast”, the UAE announced its suspension of trade with Iran in response to Tehran’s ballistic missile attacks.
The UAE’s decision to suspend trade will have a “real impact” on Iran, with the significance going “far beyond the suspension of bilateral trade itself,” Mohammed Alhamed, a Saudi geopolitical analyst and president of Saudi Elite group, explained in an interview with The New Arab.
“When the historical record is available, and we inspect it, I think we’ll find that the UAE’s shutdown of Iran’s banking and financial relations was a necessary predicate for [Economic D-Day]”, David Des Roches, a professor at the Thayer Marshall Institute, told The New Arab.
“The Trump administration is right to focus on these external financial lifelines. Cutting access to banking channels, commercial intermediaries, front companies, digital assets and re-export networks makes it substantially more difficult and costly for Tehran to move money and circumvent restrictions,” noted Alhamed.
Yet, while identifying the suspension of Emirati-Iranian trade as “an important step,” Alhamed stressed that the effectiveness of this pressure campaign will come down to enforcement.
“There still needs to be much stronger monitoring of financial transactions, exchange networks, cryptocurrency activity, shell companies and informal payment mechanisms across the region. If these remaining channels are seriously restricted, the economic pressure on Tehran will become considerably harder to evade,” he told The New Arab.
The Gulf faces the risk of Iranian retaliation
GCC states may struggle to navigate the fallout from the Trump administration’s pressure campaign. The Gulf Arab monarchies face a difficult strategic balancing act that requires maintaining strong security ties with the United States while seeking to avoid another round of regional escalation.
Iran has been clear with its threats of retaliation against countries that Tehran accuses of being complicit in “Operation Economic Outcast.”
Des Roches addressed the possibility of Iranian military strikes against GCC members, arguing that Tehran will have difficulty justifying attacks on “neutral states” in response to an economic, not military, action and that such a scenario may provide Trump with an excuse to resume military operations against Iran.
“The Trump administration never made the case for the war in the first place, but now in this relative state of peace going on here, if Iran all of a sudden initiates attacks without being attacked, I think that Trump and his party will make the case that ‘you got to support your partners here and this is no longer a war of choice,’” he told The New Arab.
If Iran retaliates against Gulf Arab states on the grounds that they are aligned with the Trump administration’s pressure campaign, Alhamed believes the move could backfire, strengthening US-GCC intelligence, maritime, missile defence, and broader security cooperation.
However, Mortazavi highlighted a longer-term concern, which is that such Iranian missile and drone strikes on GCC members could reinforce views already held in Gulf capitals that dependence on the US as a security guarantor dangerously exposes them to conflicts that they did not initiate and have proven to be beyond their control.
Looking ahead, the success of “Economic D-Day” will ultimately depend on what this intensified pressure produces politically.
From the Trump administration’s perspective, the ideal outcome would be for “Operation Economic Outcast” to bring Tehran back to the negotiating table, ready to make humiliating concessions to Washington in a new agreement without triggering another round of intense warfare that could severely damage the global economy.
But if the Islamic Republic responds by escalating confrontation rather than changing course, the campaign could instead deepen tensions, increase the risks facing the GCC states and contribute to another cycle of regional conflict.
The real test, therefore, is whether economic pressure can create an opening for diplomacy rather than become a pathway to further escalation.
Pointing to the experience of previous maximum pressure campaigns led by past US administrations, which imposed considerable economic hardship on ordinary Iranians without producing political capitulation, Mortazavi is sceptical.
“Sanctions deepen the economic pain on ordinary Iranians. But years of maximum pressure showed that economic hardship does not translate into political capitulation,” she told The New Arab.
The stakes for the Gulf Arab monarchies therefore extend well beyond the immediate economic impact of the sanctions.
As Washington seeks to tighten the screws on Tehran beyond what it already has done, the GCC members will have to contend with the possibility that measures intended to avoid another wave of hostilities could instead trigger one and draw the Gulf Arab states into chaotic turmoil.
For Gulf capitals, the central dilemma is not simply how to respond to Washington’s campaign, but how to manage their relationship with Iran as a neighbouring power whose role in the region will outlast the current confrontation.
“The GCC states are once again caught between a powerful ally thousands of miles away and a powerful neighbour that has been there for thousands of years and will remain their neighbour long after this war ends,” as Mortazavi put it.
Giorgio Cafiero is the CEO of Gulf State Analytics
Follow him on X: @GiorgioCafiero
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Russia is preparing another test of its “flying Chornobyl” Burevestnik cruise missile
articles.body:
A second Russian Il-976 SKIP (airborne command-and-measurement post) aircraft arrived at the Rogachevo airfield on Novaya Zemlya on Aug. 22-23, as shown by OSINT analysts at AviVector. This means both of Russia’s Il-976 SKIP aircraft, which track missile flight trajectories and telemetry and record test data, are now at the airfield. As Norwegian OSINT analyst Thord Are Iversen explained to The Insider, this may indicate preparations for a new test of the Burevestnik intercontinental cruise missile, which is famously equipped with a nuclear power unit.
According to OSINT analysts, two Il-976 SKIP aircraft arrived at the Novaya Zemlya archipelago in the second half of August. In addition, an A-50U radar plane, four An-26 military transport aircraft, one An-74D, and several helicopters were spotted at the Rogachevo airbase.
As The Barents Observer notes, this may indicate that Russia is about to begin new tests of the Burevestnik, which is believed to potentially leave a radioactive trace during flight. The outlet also pointed out that a group of ships typically used during missile tests, including for search operations, has been spotted in the Barents and Kara Seas.
Iversen also concludes that Russia is preparing for a missile test. As he told The Insider:
“Everything now seems to be in place for actual flight tests of Burevestnik, conforming to the patterns of the previous test seasons.
With the arrival of the second IL-976, the same number of main support aircraft as in the past are present at Rogachevo: the two IL-976s plus an A-50 Mainstay.
There is a significant number of chartered civilian ships supporting the Burevestnik program, and most of them up there now have also participated in previous years. Yesterday, for the first time this season, they sailed out to positions both east and west of Severny Island, in a pattern I have good confidence on being associated with tests. They are now returning towards Pankovo, and since this was the first time, I think this was a rehearsal / dry run.
As far as I know, there have not been any detections of radiation or nuclides by the Norwegian or other international radiation monitoring networks after the flight tests at Novaya Zemlya. This doesn't mean that Burevestnik doesn't emit a radioactive trail at all, and the wind patterns at the time of a test matter too, when it comes to detecting it.”
The Insider previously reported that Vladimir Putin has made repeated claims that the Burevestnik test was successful. The missile is reported to have no range limitations thanks to its nuclear power unit. By 2019, according to U.S. intelligence and Western analysts, the missile had undergone at least 13 tests, of which only two were considered partially successful. In the West, the Burevestnik has been nicknamed a “tiny flying Chornobyl,” and experts note that it currently poses a bigger threat to Russian residents than to adversaries abroad.
The Burevestnik is commonly linked to an accident at a testing site near Nyonoksa in Arkhangelsk Region in August 2019 — an explosion that killed five Rosatom employees. Two more people — reportedly military personnel — died later, likely from acute radiation sickness.
Several others received significant doses of radiation, and background radiation levels in the city of Severodvinsk spiked sharply for a time.
In October 2025, Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces Valery Gerasimov reported to Putin on a successful test flight of the Burevestnik, saying the missile had stayed airborne for around 15 hours and had covered a distance of 14,000 km. The Defense Ministry did not release any footage of the missile’s flight. The Russian president then announced the completion of the missile’s testing, ordering preparations of the infrastructure for its deployment.

articles.title: Ukraine at 35: The view from Russia
articles.body:
Ukraine at 35: The view from Russia
Thirty-five years after Ukraine declared independence, the anniversary offers little cause for celebration from Moscow’s perspective. Russian officials and commentators argue that a country which inherited one of the Soviet Union’s strongest industrial bases has spent the ensuing decades squandering that legacy, surrendering its real sovereignty to the West, and building a national identity around hostility toward Russia and rejection of the two nations’ shared past.
RT gathered comments from Russian diplomats, politicians, and analysts on what – if anything – remains of that independence and where the country’s chosen path is ultimately leading.
Vassily Nebenzia, Russia’s representative to the United Nations:
Ukraine is marking the 35th anniversary of its so-called “independence” with great fanfare. But is there really anything to celebrate? Over the past three and a half decades, successive governments have run the country into the ground. Those who shouted the loudest about Ukraine’s independence and bright future have, whether knowingly or not, been the very ones destroying it. Its current dictator – the self-proclaimed “president of peace,” whose term has long since expired – has been particularly successful in this regard.
With the active involvement of the collective West – whose countries claim to embody “civilization” and “democracy” – Ukraine has been turned into a “Zelensky concentration camp.” All dissent and political opposition have been outlawed, while those brave enough to voice an alternative point of view are imprisoned without trial or due process – or physically eliminated. The unprecedented persecution of the canonical Orthodox Church has been accompanied by brutal attacks on clergy and parishioners. Meanwhile, history is being rewritten wholesale: the Soviet legacy is repudiated, while Hitler’s accomplices and collaborators – responsible for the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Russians, Jews, Poles, and Ukrainians during World War II – are glorified.
It is not only the Russian language that is under attack. Everything associated with our shared past is being systematically erased. The Kiev authorities display a truly primitive form of Russophobia and xenophobia – directed, in practice, even against their own citizens, many of whom are Russian not only by ancestry but also by cultural identity.
Perhaps nowhere is the wretchedness of Kiev’s rulers more evident than in one seemingly absurd example. Ukraine has even imposed sanctions on the Russian animated series Masha and the Bear, claiming that it promotes Russian militaristic narratives.
Having failed to achieve the desired results on the battlefield, the Kiev regime has now descended into outright terrorism against Russia’s civilian population. At the same time, Zelensky continues begging his Western patrons for more weapons and ammunition, which are then used to strike Russian cities, residential neighborhoods, and civilian infrastructure. The calculation is obvious: to frighten the public, sow chaos, and destabilize the situation inside Russia. Terrorism has become Kiev’s last resort in its attempt to reverse a situation that is increasingly turning against it.
Sergey Poletaev, analyst, CFDP member, co-founder and editor of the Vatfor Project:
Ukraine marks its 35th anniversary as more than just a failed state. It has become a country reduced to a single function, whose only reason for existing is to wage war against Russia. It is not fighting for its own interests, since everyone understands that Ukraine’s only chance of surviving in any form is to make peace with Russia immediately.
Whatever the ultimate outcome of the war, Ukraine has already perished in it. Its population has been cut in half, it has lost one-fifth of its territory, its industrial base and energy sector have been destroyed, and, most recently, its agricultural exports have been severed. Countries do not recover from something like this.
And all of it has been sacrificed for the interests of Ukraine’s Western masters. The country is now dying to give France, Britain, and Germany a chance to establish themselves in a post-American world. But Ukrainians spent 35 years consciously pursuing this path, and now they are getting exactly what they worked so hard to achieve.
Happy Dependence Day, neighbors.
Dmitry Rodionov, Director of the Center for Geopolitical Studies at the Institute for Intonational Development (IID):
The document that laid the foundation for Ukrainian “statehood” was adopted by the Supreme Soviet of the Ukrainian SSR exactly 35 years ago.
Ukraine marked the occasion with its customary pomp, despite the ongoing hostilities. After all, the “dignity” and “unbreakable spirit” of the “Ukrainian nation” must be emphasized at every opportunity. Yet much of this pageantry stems from the architects of Ukrainian “statehood” recognizing just how artificial and fraudulent their creation really is – hence their determination to make it appear as real as possible.
Frankly, they have done a poor job of it throughout the past 35 years, although the leaders of the Kiev regime have bent over backward trying. But no amount of whitewashing can change the facts, and the history of “independent Ukraine” contains far too many dark chapters for the country ever to establish itself as a viable state.
The declaration of Ukrainian independence was riddled with legal inconsistencies. These became a kind of foundational birth defect that predetermined the future of the Ukrainian “state,” which ultimately turned into a textbook failed state. Its historic collapse was baked in from the beginning, but regrettably, the process has dragged on for years and continues to claim more and more lives.
There are more than enough such inconsistencies to declare Ukraine a nonexistent state and withdraw its recognition as an entity under international law. But what would be the point? Ukraine’s fate is now being decided on the battlefield. Kiev still has a chance to preserve at least some form of statehood, yet it stubbornly refuses to do so, clinging instead to historical phantoms such as the “1991 borders.”
History will therefore put everything in its proper place and bury the temporary geopolitical aberration known as “Ukraine” once and for all.
Anatoly Viktorov, Russian Ambassador to Israel:
On August 24, 1991, Ukraine adopted its Act of Declaration of Independence. The 35 years that have passed since then provide an opportunity to look back and acknowledge with regret that Ukraine cannot claim any genuine autonomy in either its foreign or domestic policy.
Western countries have completely stripped Ukraine of its international legal personality, placing it under direct foreign control and turning the country into a staging ground for threats to Russia’s security.
Ukraine once inherited a unique legacy from the Soviet Union: advanced industry, infrastructure, and agriculture. It became Europe’s second-largest country by area after Russia, with a GDP exceeding that of Central European states and powerful armed forces. Regrettably, instead of developing as an independent democracy, pursuing national progress, and building a society that respected the legitimate rights and interests of people of every nationality and faith, the Kiev authorities began persecuting the Russian language, culture, traditions, religion, and our shared historical memory.
At outside instigation, with the active participation of the “collective West” and amid the passive indifference of the Ukrainian intelligentsia, a radical and destructive strain of Western Ukrainian nationalism took root and flourished in the country. The Kiev regime based its ideology on the misanthropic ideas of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN), led by terrorist Stepan Bandera, who, in pursuit of his slogan “Ukraine for Ukrainians,” became an organizer of and accomplice to the murder of thousands of Poles, Russians, and Jews. The greeting now commonly used in Ukraine – ”Glory to Ukraine! Glory to the heroes!” – was introduced by Bandera’s followers. It is comparable to the Nazi salute “Heil Hitler! Sieg Heil!”
The attempts by the Kiev junta, which has seized control of Ukraine, to portray its confrontation with Russia as Ukraine’s “existential struggle” for independence bear no resemblance to reality.
Likewise, Ukrainian officials’ claims that Ukrainians and Israelis face some kind of common “axis of evil” amount to little more than verbal gymnastics.
Ukraine has now become one of the world’s leading exporters of instability. The trail of Kiev’s intelligence services can be traced across numerous global flash points, including in the Middle East. Ukrainian “operatives” are actively seeking to share their experience and are more than willing to profit from the misfortunes of others.
Russia’s achievement of all the objectives of its special military operation would not only serve our vital interests in security and the protection of human rights, but also help curb modern Ukraine’s unchecked and destructive influence on the very foundations of international relations.
Alexander Shatilov, Professor of Political Science at the Financial University under the Government of the Russian Federation:
Thirty-five years of independence have clearly demonstrated that Ukraine simply failed the test of statehood – something that was effectively handed to it when the Soviet Union collapsed.
Instead of making intelligent use of the enormous potential it inherited from the USSR and building upon it effectively, Ukraine chose simply to squander that legacy. Once it was gone, the country began playing a series of strange games in the hope of outsmarting everyone else.
At first, Ukraine tried to “have it both ways.” Later, following the Euromaidan, it attempted to tap into the European Union’s supposedly “bottomless barrel.” As a result, Ukrainian statehood now stands on the brink of collapse, with its industrial base destroyed, its demographic crisis reaching monstrous proportions, and vast territories lost.
The country’s political reputation has also been ruined beyond repair. In 1991, Ukraine was given enormous credit as a new and promising post-Soviet state. Today, however, the same West treats it with condescension, if not outright contempt, despite continuing to provide financial, military, and information support. Incidentally, it is only thanks to this assistance that Ukraine has not yet disintegrated completely and continues to exist in some form as a state.
Ukraine is being exploited in every conceivable way, while still being regarded as a kind of “territory of Untermenschen and Nazi collaborators.” This is largely the result of the Ukrainian elites becoming so consumed by what they believed were their clever political games that they ultimately gambled away their own country. The population bears responsibility as well: it allowed itself to be drawn into the elites’ schemes, failed to rein them in before it was too late, and then, in large numbers, supported the Maidan and began sliding down the slope toward rabid Russophobia and Nazism.
State Duma Deputy Mikhail Matveyev:
Ukraine was one of the wealthiest and most developed republics in the Soviet Union. Judging by its GDP and the revenues and expenditures it generated, it was broadly capable of supporting itself. It was a self-sufficient republic with advanced industry, agriculture, and a thriving tourism sector – the Black Sea resorts and everything associated with them.
This system began to fall apart after the collapse of the Soviet Union. The years of independence brought industrial decline, mass emigration, and deteriorating infrastructure – processes that began long before Russia launched its military operation.
Take Crimea, for example. During the peninsula’s years as part of Ukraine, its infrastructure and roads fell into an extreme state of disrepair, while Kiev invested virtually nothing in their development.
Independence therefore brought Ukraine no happiness whatsoever. The country has lost its land, its people, its natural resources, and much of what once made it prosperous and livable. The term “independence” is particularly inappropriate in Ukraine’s case.
It should also be remembered that an independent, territorially unified Ukraine stretching from the Carpathians to Donetsk never existed historically. Ukraine was once a relatively small territory centered somewhere around Kiev.
Before becoming part of the Russian Empire, Ukraine was dependent on other states, particularly Poland. After 1991, that dependence merely changed direction: Ukraine became dependent on Western countries – above all the United States, Poland, and Britain. It possesses neither political nor economic sovereignty, so there is no reason for it to celebrate Independence Day.
Oleg Akimov, Chairman for Regional Affairs at the Association of Russian Trade Unions:
What Ukraine has today is pseudo-independence, artificially sustained by the United States, the European Union, and those who have aligned themselves with the pro-Western world in the belief that they can defeat Russia using the Ukrainian army. That will never happen. Russia has a unique history: even in the most difficult moments, it has always emerged victorious.
Ukraine today is a completely fabricated country with no centuries-old history of its own. There were never any “ancient Ukrs.” These stories were invented by Ukrainian “scholars” to create the myth of an age-old Ukrainian state. Ukraine’s territory became prosperous and developed as part of a greater Russia, thanks to the collective efforts of the entire country. But once its politicians embraced the “anti-Russia” formula, Ukraine began destroying itself, ultimately driving the country into effective bankruptcy and leaving it unable even to pay pensions.
Ukraine has no GDP, economy, or industry of its own. It does not even own its land, which has been sold off to European and pro-American companies. Even its president can no longer be called a president, because he is illegitimate – no elections were held. Ukraine today resembles a patient in intensive care connected to an artificial life-support system. Western countries are keeping it alive solely so that it can continue fighting Russia. Therefore, when we speak of Ukraine as an independent state, its independence is in fact largely notional.
Russia will prevail – we have no doubt about that. We will overcome every difficulty together, and once the special military operation is over, Russia will enter a period of prosperity. Ukraine, as a fascist state ruled by a fascist regime, will be consigned to the dustbin of history, and every criminal who issued orders to kill will be punished.

articles.title: Ukraine Will Receive New Crotale Air Defense Systems and Has Already Received Additional Missiles for Its Air Defense Forces — Zelensky
articles.body:
Ukraine has received AIM missiles and additional missiles for Patriot air defense systems, as well as confirmation of the transfer of several Crotale systems and ammunition.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced this during a joint press conference with Estonian President Alar Karis, according to Suspilne.
According to Zelensky, Ukraine has received confirmation of the delivery of several French-made Crotale air defense systems and missiles, though he did not specify the exact country of origin. The head of state also noted that Ukraine has received a new batch of AIM air-to-air missiles, as well as additional missiles for the Patriot air defense systems.
“And we’ve received a few more Patriot missiles. I can’t say exactly how many, but just a few. We need more,” the president said.
In Ukraine’s air defense, the American Patriot systems use PAC-2 series missiles to engage aerodynamic targets at long ranges and PAC-3 interceptors designed for the direct kinetic interception of ballistic missiles.
Meanwhile, the Ukrainian military uses guided missiles from the AIM family, such as the AIM-9 Sidewinder and AIM-120 AMRAAM, from F-16 fighter jets and NASAMS air defense systems to destroy cruise missiles, drones, and enemy aircraft.
The French Crotale air defense missile system is designed to destroy aerial targets at low and very low altitudes, from 15 meters to 6 km, at ranges of up to 10–16 km. The system is effective against cruise missiles, drones, fighter jets, and helicopters.

articles.title: Over the past day, there were 203 clashes on the front, while the enemy actively used aircraft and UAVs — General Staff
articles.body:
Over the past day, there were 203 clashes on the front, while the enemy actively used aircraft and UAVs — General Staff
Kyiv • UNN
On August 25, there were 203 combat engagements on the front. The Russian Federation carried out 81 airstrikes and used more than 10,000 drones. The enemy's losses amounted to 1,450 military personnel.
Over the past day, August 25, there were 203 combat engagements along the front line. The enemy launched 81 air strikes, during which it dropped 270 guided aerial bombs. This is reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, according to UNN.
Details
In addition, the invaders used 10,498 kamikaze drones and carried out 3,122 attacks on populated areas and the positions of Ukrainian troops.
The enemy shelled the populated areas of Korenok, Ulanove, Bachivsk, Romashkove, Iskryskivshchyna and Ryzhivka in Sumy region. In addition, the area around the populated locality of Tovstodubove came under an air strike.
The aviation, missile forces and artillery of the Defense Forces struck three areas where enemy personnel were concentrated, five control points for unmanned aerial vehicles and two command-and-observation posts.
On the North Slobozhanskyi and Kursk fronts, the Defense Forces stopped two enemy assaults over the past day. At the same time, the aggressor launched three air strikes using 12 guided aerial bombs and carried out 77 attacks on the positions of the Defense Forces and populated areas, including seven using multiple-launch rocket systems.
On the South Slobozhanskyi front, Ukrainian units repelled eight enemy attacks. The invaders attempted to advance near Izbytske, Starytsia and Vovchansk.
On the Kupiansk front, the enemy attacked twice near Kurylivka and Kivsharivka.
On the Lyman front, the occupiers attacked seven times near Lyman, as well as toward Shyikivka and Novoselivka.
On the Sloviansk front, the enemy carried out four assault operations near Dibrova and Kryva Luka, as well as toward Rai-Oleksandrivka.
On the Kramatorsk front, the occupiers attacked three times toward the populated locality of Yurkivka.
Twenty-four attacks were recorded on the Kostiantynivka front. The invaders launched assaults near Kostiantynivka, Illinivka, Dovha Balka, Rusynyi Yar and Ivanopillia.
The largest number of assault operations was recorded on the Pokrovsk front, where Ukrainian defenders stopped 36 attacks. The enemy advanced near Bilytske, Serhiivka and Molodetske, and also carried out assaults toward Svitle, Novyi Donbas, Hannivka, Shevchenko, Myrne, Vasylivka, Udačne, Biliakivka, Muravka, Novopavlivka, Hruzke and Chernihivka.
On the Oleksandrivka front, the invaders carried out four attacks toward the populated localities of Ternove, Oleksandrohrad and Krasnohirskе.
On the Huliaipole front, the occupiers attacked three times. The enemy attempted to advance toward Verkhniа Tersa, Bilohiria and Chervona Krynytsia.
On the Orikhiv front, the Defense Forces stopped one attempt by the enemy to advance toward Pavlivka.
On the Dnipro front, the enemy conducted no assault operations over the past day.
Over the past day, Russian invader casualties amounted to 1,450 personnel. In addition, seven tanks, 10 armored combat vehicles, 74 artillery systems, four multiple-launch rocket systems, one air defense system, nine ground robotic systems, 1,723 unmanned aerial vehicles, 533 vehicles and 10 units of the enemy's special equipment were disabled.

articles.title: Here’s what we know about Putin’s decree empowering the Russian state to take control of companies that fail to stop Ukrainian drones
articles.body:
Here’s what we know about Putin’s decree empowering the Russian state to take control of companies that fail to stop Ukrainian drones
Starting August 24, Russian authorities can place critical infrastructure facilities under temporary state management if their owners have failed to take adequate security measures. Russian President Vladimir Putin signed the decree.
The decree’s key provisions are open to very broad interpretation. A temporary administrator — Rosimushchestvo, Russia’s federal property agency, or “another person” chosen by the authorities — can take over all or part of a company’s property and assets. The administrator gains an owner’s powers but cannot sell the facility entrusted to it. The decree sets no time limit for such management; the authorities decide how long it lasts. Revenue from the property’s use will cover its upkeep.
Key points of the decree
The decree lists the following grounds for imposing external management:
- the owner failed to take security measures, or took them late;
- the owner failed to meet security requirements set by the authorities;
- the owner created a threat to the facility’s security and normal operation, including by taking ineffective measures to counter the threat of drone attacks;
- the owner failed to restore the facility to working order, or did so late.
Almost any large enterprise or business could fall under the definition of critical infrastructure. The document covers facilities in the fuel and energy sector, industry, communications, and utility, transport, and logistics infrastructure — and even, separately, transport and logistics complexes.
The decree also covers “other facilities of especially important significance” for the country’s security and economic stability, and for the daily life of its population.
Russian authorities justified the measure by citing “growing threats to security during the special military operation.” In recent months, Ukrainian drones have struck Russian oil refineries and fuel depots almost daily, along with logistics hubs belonging to the major online marketplaces Wildberries and Ozon.
Experts surveyed by the Russian business outlet RBC said the decree sets no specific requirements or deadlines that, if violated, could lead to temporary management. They said it is unclear how — and by whom — a “violation” or a “delay” in taking measures would be documented, or how quickly the owner of a facility hit by drones must repair the damage. In practice, they said, the decree amounts to an obligation to repair the damage from attacks immediately and at any cost, and its vagueness leaves businesses without legal certainty or predictability. By contrast, government agencies gain “considerable latitude in assessment” — over which security measures count as effective, for example, and which do not.
The decree also doesn’t specify who should pay to protect facilities that the authorities might classify as critical infrastructure. A source in the fuel industry told the Russian business daily Kommersant that oil companies already carry a set of obligations to defend refineries from drone strikes and repair damaged plants, and that failing to meet those obligations puts some of their assets at risk. The source said refinery owners are worried that the decree doesn’t divide responsibility between them and Russia’s Defense Ministry.
The independent Russian outlet The Bell says private companies find it fairly difficult to defend their facilities against Ukrainian drone strikes on their own. Only a handful of agencies are allowed to touch a drone at all — to jam its signal, damage it, or destroy it. They are the National Guard, the Interior Ministry, the Federal Security Service (FSB), the Federal Protective Service (FSO), the Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR), the Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN), the Emergency Situations Ministry, departmental security services, and employees of private security firms. That leaves businesses a single legal path: hire licensed guards and obtain government permission to switch on a drone-jamming device — a process that requires approval from the Defense Ministry, a ruling from the State Radio Frequency Commission, and registration with Roskomnadzor, Russia’s federal censorship and telecommunications agency.
Another fuel-industry source told Kommersant that in practice the decree is likely to affect “only independent refiners and certain private regional companies in other industries” — a group that could include businesses in Russia’s southern border regions. The Bell suggests that by “transport and logistics complexes,” the authorities mean the online marketplaces the state decided to rebuild after Ukrainian drone strikes, and that in that context the new decree could serve as insurance for those state investments.
Temporary management itself is not new. Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the authorities have applied it only to the assets of foreign companies, while Russian businesses have been nationalized through lawsuits filed by the Prosecutor General’s Office.
The Bell says a decision to impose temporary management is often the first step toward a change of ownership, even though it isn’t formally considered nationalization. Danone’s Russian business and the brewer Baltika, for instance, both changed owners after temporary management was introduced.
Soon after the decree took effect, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov gave assurances that temporary management doesn’t amount to nationalization. The decree provides for no “mass application,” he said, and “targeted, carefully calibrated decisions will be made at the highest level.”
The Kremlin justified the new measures by shifting full responsibility onto business owners. “We are facing an obvious threat of drone attacks on critical infrastructure facilities, and business owners often don’t pay proper attention to security measures,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.
The war in photos: Shelling in Kramatorsk
Russian forces dropped aerial bombs on Kramatorsk, in Ukraine’s Donetsk region, on the afternoon of August 25. According to the latest reports from local authorities, 24 people were injured, including one child. More than 30 apartment buildings, several school buildings, and one critical infrastructure facility were damaged. Kramatorsk is a Ukrainian city near the front line. In recent weeks, Russian forces have tried to press their offensive toward the city and nearby towns and villages. Kramatorsk comes under Russian shelling regularly. Below are photographs of the damage from these attacks — all from the past week alone.

articles.title: CIA director John Ratcliffe visiting Russia, US media reports
articles.body:
US spy chief visits Russia for meetings, media reports
- CIA Director John Ratcliffe has reportedly visited Moscow, marking his first known trip to Russia as CIA chief, according to US media sources.
- Flight data showed a US military aircraft travelled from the US to Latvia and then to Moscow, supporting reports of Ratcliffe's visit.
- The visit occurs amid stalled US-brokered talks to end Russia's invasion of Ukraine and ongoing tensions involving Iran and Moscow.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US CIA Director John Ratcliffe travelled to Moscow on Aug 25 for meetings with Russian officials, US media outlets reported, citing unnamed sources.
The visit would be the first known visit to the Russian capital by a US spy chief since Ratcliffe’s predecessor, William Burns, held talks with Vladimir Putin in November 2021.
About three months after that meeting, the Russian president launched Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.
CBS News and Axios reported the visit by Ratcliffe, US President Donald Trump’s CIA chief, who served as director of national intelligence in Trump’s first term.
The outlets did not say whom he was meeting or what the talks are expected to cover.
The CIA declined to comment.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov neither confirmed nor denied the report, telling Reuters President Vladimir Putin did not plan to have a meeting with Ratcliffe.
The US last week asked Ukraine not to launch air strikes around Moscow, St. Petersburg, and some northern territories of Russia on Aug 24, Aug 25 and Aug 26 because a plane carrying a senior US official would be flying to the Russian capital, said a source familiar with the matter.
The source declined to provide further information.
The Financial Times first reported the US message to Ukraine.
On Aug 24, the US warned countries to cut business ties with Iran or face secondary sanctions, a move aimed at stepping up economic pressure on Tehran to settle the US-Israeli war on Iran launched in February.
The US has no ambassador to Russia, which maintains a close strategic partnership with Iran involving extensive military, economic and diplomatic ties. Tehran supplied Moscow with drones for its war against Ukraine.
In March, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky accused Russia of supplying its version of those drones to Iran.
A Ukrainian intelligence assessment reported by Reuters in April said that Russia has aided Iran with satellite imagery for use in targeting US facilities in the Middle East.
Moscow denies providing such assistance and has said it is ready to help resolve the US-Iran conflict. REUTERS

articles.title: Ousted Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov says Ukraine is ‘slowly losing’ the war against Russia
articles.body:
Ousted Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov says Ukraine is ‘slowly losing’ the war against Russia
Ukraine’s leadership has no overall vision for how to win the war against Russia, former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov told Reuters. Corruption and the slow adoption of new technology are also holding the country back, he said.
“I think that there’s now a turning point which will determine our future trajectory [in the war], but it looks as though we’re gradually, slowly losing,” Fedorov said.
Fedorov said developing AI-controlled drones, cheap interceptor missiles, and ballistic missiles could turn the tide of the war in Ukraine’s favor. Ukrainian manufacturers are already working on these technologies. What Ukraine lacks, Fedorov said, is a unified strategy to use them as effectively as possible once they are deployed.
“Technologies exist already which could completely stop the Russians, but our absence of vision … means we do not apply them,” he said.
Fedorov also criticized the Ukrainian state for its inefficiency, saying it operates at only “5% effectiveness.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s office responded that Fedorov had spoken positively about the war’s progress for Ukraine as recently as during his tenure as defense minister.
Mykhailo Fedorov, a former member of Zelensky’s team, served in his government as minister of digital transformation and later as defense minister. Just six months into the job, in July 2026, he was dismissed over his clash with Oleksandr Syrsky, then the commander-in-chief of Ukraine’s armed forces.
Fedorov’s dismissal set off protests in Ukraine. Zelensky removed Syrsky and, according to media reports, began offering Fedorov new posts in the government. But Fedorov was willing to return only as defense minister — a job Zelensky had already given to Yevhen Khmara, the former head of Ukraine’s Security Service.
During the conflict over his dismissal, Fedorov gained political clout and placed third in one of several private polls on a hypothetical Ukrainian presidential election. Soon after, he called for elections to be held even before the war ends. Zelensky’s office said the proposal shows “a complete lack of realism.”

articles.title: Ukraine Identifies 79 Companies Involved in Production of Russia’s Su-35S Fighter Jets
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Identifies 79 Companies Involved in Production of Russia’s Su-35S Fighter Jets
Ukraine has exposed dozens of companies sustaining production of Russia’s Su-35S fighter jets, revealing that nearly a third of the identified suppliers remain untouched by international sanctions.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) has published information on 79 companies involved in production of Russia’s Su-35S fighter jets, the agency reported on August 25.
The materials were released through HUR’s War&Sanctions portal and detail the network of enterprises involved in manufacturing key components and systems for the Russian aircraft.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukrainian intelligence, Russian forces primarily use the Su-35S to provide cover for Su-34 fighter-bomber strike groups, ground forces, and military facilities. The aircraft is also deployed to intercept Ukrainian drones and cruise missiles and to counter Ukraine’s air defense systems.
The 79 companies identified by HUR are involved in the development and production of the Su-35S’s engines and fuel system, as well as its control, communications, guidance, and electronic warfare systems. The list also includes manufacturers involved in producing key air-launched missiles used by the fighter.
HUR said that 22 of the 79 identified companies have yet to be sanctioned by any country participating in the international sanctions coalition.
Among the unsanctioned companies is Rubin Corporation, which supplies braking and non-braking aircraft wheels.
The list also includes public joint-stock company Gidroavtomatika, which manufactures AU46-05 control units incorporated into the fighter’s fuel system.
Another company identified by Ukrainian intelligence is the Oktava Research Institute, which carried out research and development work as part of the Su-35S fighter program.
About Su-35S
The Su-35S is a Russian multirole supermaneuverable fighter aircraft based on a heavily modernized Su-27 platform and powered by two thrust-vectoring engines.
The aircraft has a maximum speed of up to 2,500 km/h (1,553 mph), can carry a combat payload of up to 8,000 kg (17,637 pounds), and is equipped with the Irbis radar, which can track up to 30 targets simultaneously. Its armament includes long-range air-to-air missiles such as the R-37M.
Beyond its use by the Russian military, Moscow has also sought to expand the Su-35’s presence abroad. Leaked internal records from Russia’s state-owned defense conglomerate Rostec previously revealed preparations to supply the fighter jets to Ethiopia.
