A High Mobility Artillery Rocket System platoon from the New Hampshire Army National Guard’s 3-197th Field Artillery Regiment will provide a precision fires element, while US Air Force Special Operations Command MC-130 and US Air Forces Europe C-130 aircraft will support air mobility and rapid insertion. Elements of the US Navy’s Sixth Fleet and Task Force 68 are also participating.
Norway will contribute personnel from the Royal Norwegian Navy and Norwegian Home Guard. The British contingent consists of RAF personnel and Royal Marines, although the US announcement does not detail the number of UK personnel involved or specify the exact aircraft and Commando Force capabilities being deployed.
Vice Admiral Rune Andersen, Commander of the Norwegian Joint Headquarters, said: “By operating alongside our Allies, we demonstrate that we have both the capability and the will to defend Norwegian territory. This includes the Arctic islands, the High North and our territorial waters.”
Jan Mayen’s position gives the exercise a particular maritime focus. The volcanic Norwegian island lies in the Norwegian Sea to the north of the GIUK Gap, the broad maritime approaches between Greenland, Iceland and the United Kingdom that connect the North Atlantic with northern European waters. Those routes are strategically important for movement between North America and Europe and have long featured in NATO planning for surveillance, reinforcement and anti-submarine operations.
Operation Atlantic City will take place at the same time as naval manoeuvres associated with Northern Viking 26, allowing participating forces to make use of overlapping maritime surveillance and sensing activity. Northern Viking is centred on Iceland and the strategically important sea routes through the GIUK Gap, while Atlantic City pushes elements of the wider Arctic Sentry activity farther north onto Norwegian territory.
Major General Frode Kristoffersen, Deputy Chief of Staff for Operations at Joint Force Command Norfolk, described the wider purpose of the NATO activity, saying: “Arctic Sentry is our way of synchronizing all Arctic activity conducted by Allies to increase Arctic security, gain the most deterrent effect possible from those activities, and make sure that we have increased our common situational awareness in the Arctic.”
The deployment will also test the more mundane but critical challenges of operating from an isolated Arctic location. Forces on Jan Mayen must contend with long supply lines, limited infrastructure, difficult weather and rapidly changing environmental conditions. Moving personnel, sensors and weapons onto the island and sustaining them there is therefore part of the operational problem being exercised alongside targeting and command integration.
For the British contingent, the exercise will provide another opportunity to integrate Royal Marines and RAF personnel with US and Norwegian forces in the High North while NATO develops procedures for operating dispersed forces across the Arctic and the northern approaches to the GIUK Gap.

articles.title: Indian national security adviser holds border talks in China
articles.body:
Indian national security adviser holds border talks in China
Indian National Security Adviser Ajit Doval held talks with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi on Tuesday on the border issue between the two countries and improving relations.
”We are meeting in keeping with the guidance of our leaders, Prime Minister Narendra Modi and President Xi Jinping, who have given clear and positive direction to our relationship, both at the highest and working levels,” Doval said in his remarks, reports said. “I am happy that, over the past year, our relationship has been steadily returning to normalcy.”
Doval noted that the talks are “particularly important against the backdrop of the BRICS Summit.” The summit will be held in New Delhi next month and Chinese President Xi Jinping will reportedly attend.
The two officials are the designated special representatives for the border talks mechanism, which was established in 2003. It is the main channel for negotiations between the two countries on the border issue and communication on issues of mutual interest.
Doval, who is on a two-day visit to China, met with Chinese Vice President Han Zheng on Monday and discussed ways to strengthen peace in the border areas and improve economic, political, and multilateral relations, the Indian Embassy said in an X post.
National Security Advisor Ajit Doval held the 25th round of Special Representatives’ talks on the India-China boundary question with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing.
During his visit, NSA Doval also met Chinese Vice President Han Zheng, with discussions focusing on… pic.twitter.com/QyEcnOaYN3
Ahead of the talks, Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar reiterated that “peace and tranquility” along the border areas are a prerequisite for good relations with China.
Relations between the two nuclear-armed neighbors froze after a skirmish between their troops in the Ladakh region of their common Himalayan border in 2020, which left 20 Indian soldiers and at least four Chinese soldiers dead.
The two countries have been rapidly normalizing relations recently, with the resumption of direct flights and updates to the visa regime. India has started allowing Chinese investments into critical sectors of its economy. Border trade, which once connected remote Himalayan communities to the Silk Route, was also resumed earlier this month.
Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to attend the BRICS summit in New Delhi next month with a 400-strong delegation, Reuters reported, citing three unnamed sources.
Xi’s participation in the summit, which Russian President Vladimir Putin will also attend, has not been officially confirmed yet. India, which holds the rotating chair of the BRICS group, has engaged in intense diplomacy ahead of the summit.

articles.title: From Colombia to Venezuela, Palestine is a global litmus test
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
From Colombia to Venezuela, Palestine is a global litmus test
This month, Venezuela revived consular services with Israel after severing diplomatic relations 17 years ago, while Colombia went beyond, recognising Israel’s sovereignty over the Syrian Golan Heights it occupied in 1967 and annexed in 1981. Both moves should be read as declarations of ideological alignment.
Venezuela has not yet restored full diplomatic relations, which the late Hugo Chávez severed in 2009 during Israel’s war on Gaza. The recent channel grew out of Israeli assistance following Venezuela’s earthquake. Yet Israel’s foreign minister immediately celebrated it as a diplomatic success.
Colombia’s decision is more obscene. Until Bogotá’s announcement, only Donald Trump’s United States had recognised Israeli sovereignty over the territory. Gustavo Petro had broken relations with Israel in 2024 over the Gaza genocide. However, only days after the right-wing Abelardo de la Espriella took office, his government restored ties and security cooperation with Israel and recognised Israel’s Golan annexation claim.
His incoming foreign minister had already met Gideon Saar in Washington, where they agreed to appoint ambassadors, eliminate visa requirements and move Colombia’s embassy to Jerusalem. De la Espriella had called for Colombia to acquire advanced weapons, drones and technology from Israel and the United States.
David and Goliath
We have just watched the same play in Slovenia. A centre-left government recognised Palestine, sanctioned Benjamin Netanyahu and two far-right Israeli ministers, banned imports of settlements and imposed an arms embargo. When Janez Janša’s conservative government arrived, it scrapped those measures, removed the Palestinian flag from a government building and reopened the door to Israel.
This shift in domestic power in three states—two in Latin America and one in Europe—produced an immediate policy shift towards Palestine. This is hardly a coincidence. Palestine is a global political litmus test.
Whenever the left is rising, the Palestinian flag is rarely far away. It appears at a small anti-racist protest in an American town, at campaigns challenging the power of money and lobbies in congressional races, and among the progressive ultras of Celtic, who have repeatedly defied their club and UEFA to turn the stands green, white, red and black.
It flew in Tahrir Square, where solidarity with the Palestinian Intifada had helped educate generations of Egyptian activists long before the 2011 revolution.
The flag appears because Palestine condenses the central questions confronting every emancipatory movement. Who is the underdog resisting the powers that be? Who is the little David fighting the giant Goliath? Who is entitled to control the land and decide who lives and who dies?
Any person or political movement struggling to change society with a progressive vision starts drawing parallels with other struggles over similar causes elsewhere and begins to understand how they are connected.
Is it a coincidence that Egyptian striking workers on the eve of the revolution accused the riot police of behaving like Israelis when they suspended by force their sit-in around the parliament? Is it a coincidence that Greta Thunberg began fighting against climate change only to swiftly connect the dots and sail to Gaza?
The reverse pattern is equally visible. When reaction, conservatism and fascism advance, Israel’s flag often follows.
Far-right and Israel
Israeli flags have appeared at Tommy Robinson’s anti-migration mobilisations in Britain, including a 2024 rally where the crowd booed a Palestinian flag. For Germany’s AfD and Europe’s far right—certainly some of the worst antisemites on the planet—support for Israel runs high because the admiration is for walls, militarised borders, demographic engineering, and a state organised around ethnic supremacy.
American white nationalist Richard Spencer made the logic explicit when he called himself a “white Zionist”, presenting Israel as a model for the white ethnostate he desired. The far right sees no contradiction between its hatred toward Jews at home and support for Israel. The latter offers a worldview which embodies the far right’s wildest dreams: minorities separated, migrants expelled, and each population confined to its supposed place.
Latin America has seen first-hand this worldview in action. During the Cold War, Israel armed and assisted right-wing regimes fighting revolutionary dissent, from Somoza’s Nicaragua to the Guatemalan military during its counterinsurgency war. It developed lasting security relationships with governments and armed forces in Colombia, Argentina, and elsewhere.
When the US faced legal constraints, Israel stepped in to supply weapons, training and intelligence to its allies. Such a partnership was natural. Israel and the juntas shared a view of popular movements as enemies to be surveilled, displaced or eliminated.
The same logic is at play today. Washington reasserts its domination over Caracas, and a government born from US intervention opens a channel with Israel. A Colombian administration eager to restore intimacy with Trump restores relations with Israel and endorses Trump’s Golan decree.
Janša, another Trump admirer, takes Slovenia to the right and begins dismantling its Palestine policy. In each case, alignment with the United States carries an Israeli entrance fee.
This is why Palestine is more than just a local conflict in the Middle East. A country at the far end of the world that wishes to identify with US imperial power is expected to make peace with Zionism. It buys Israeli weapons, repeats Israeli security narratives, and treats Palestinian rights as disposable. In so many ways, Israel is the quickest and most important gateway into the reactionary club.
Victories for progressive forces are therefore essential to keeping Israel isolated and making its leaders pay a political price for occupation, apartheid and genocide. Every election that defeats the far right, every successful anti-racist mobilisation and every workplace or university that adopts boycott and divestment helps keep Palestine visible.
Latin America shows what happens when power shifts to the right. But power shifts because people actively push it. Palestine remains the flag that tells us who is pushing, in which direction, and towards what kind of world.
Hossam el-Hamalawy is an Egyptian scholar-activist in Germany, focusing on the military, policing, and labour.
Follow Hossam on X: @3arabawy
Have questions or comments? Email us at editorial-english@newarab.com
Opinions expressed in this article remain those of the author and do not necessarily represent those of The New Arab.

articles.title: US-led Gaza peace board warns Hamas over kites after Israeli threat
articles.body:
US-led Gaza peace board warns Hamas over kites after Israeli threat
The US-led board overseeing the Gaza peace plan warned Hamas on Tuesday to halt militant activity, including flying kites, after Israel threatened retaliatory strikes. A Board of Peace official said Israel must also respect the ceasefire, limiting military action to responses to “genuine and imminent threats.”
The US-led board supervising a Gaza peace plan on Tuesday warned Hamas against flying kites, after Israel threatened retaliatory strikes.
"All militant activity in Gaza must stop, including the flying of kites. We have conveyed this message directly through the established mechanism," an official on President Donald Trump's "Board of Peace" said on condition of anonymity.
"Israel, too, must comply with the ceasefire. Military action cannot extend beyond responding to genuine and imminent threats," the official said.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday warned Hamas that Israel would step up operations in Gaza if it launches kites, drones or balloons.
Read moreTrump's Board of Peace reassures Israel after objections on Gaza pullout plan
The threat came after a series of kites reportedly were found across the Gaza border in southern Israel, communities traumatised by the Hamas-led attacks of October 7, 2023.
The episode revived memories of incendiary kites and balloons once launched from Gaza. The latest kites are not known to have had any explosives, although Israeli media reported at least one with a political message.
Hamas political bureau member Basem Naim voiced outrage at the warning on kites conveyed via the Board of Peace.
"What audacity! Is it conceivable that attempts to appease the war criminal Netanyahu have led them to describe innocent children's activities as armed activities, while Netanyahu continues to kill and destroy daily despite the agreement?"
The United Nations earlier Tuesday described the Israeli threats over the kites as unacceptable.
"On the threat of expulsion due to children's kite flying, I hope we can all agree that this is outrageous," UN rights office spokeswoman Ravina Shamdasani told reporters in Geneva.
Read moreWhat we know about the Hamas disarmament deal announced by Trump
The Board of Peace was put in place by Trump to oversee a ceasefire declared in October in the bloody conflict in Gaza.
Since then, Israel has expanded slightly further into Gaza and kept up strikes, which have killed 1,288 Palestinians, according to health authorities under Hamas whose figures are generally considered reliable by the UN.
On Monday, Gaza authorities said Israeli fire killed at least five people including two children.
Netanyahu, facing tight elections in October, earlier this month rejected the latest stage in the Gaza peace plan after Hamas said it had agreed to disarm.
Netanyahu voiced scepticism over the promises and told Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner last week that a US general should be placed in charge of verifying the destruction of all Hamas's weapons.
In response to Netanyahu, the Board of Peace backtracked and assured him that Israeli troops need not leave Gaza until a complete demilitarisation of Hamas. Earlier the board had called for Israel to start a phased withdrawal.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

articles.title: Strategic vacuum: Why is Trump's economic warfare against Iran doomed to fail?
articles.body:
Strategic vacuum: Why is Trump's economic warfare against Iran doomed to fail?
TEHRAN- Six months into his military campaign against Iran, Donald Trump finds himself trapped in the very quagmire he promised to eliminate. What began as a boastful declaration of "decisive action" to crush Iran and effect regime change has devolved into a strategic fiasco that not only fails to achieve its objectives but is inflicting profound damage on the U.S. economy and global stability. The administration's latest gambit—announcing the "largest financial attack in history" against Iran on August 24, a self-styled "D-Day" of economic warfare—appears less a stroke of genius and more an act of desperation from a presidency with no viable strategy left.
The irony is palpable. As U.S. Treasury officials threaten economic Armageddon against Tehran, America's own energy reserves are collapsing. Official data from July 2026 reveals that U.S. crude oil stockpiles, including the Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR), have plummeted to their lowest level in half a century—just 41 days of coverage, compared to the historical average of 65 days. Washington has depleted its most powerful tool for market intervention, leaving itself exposed to any future supply shock. This is not strength; this is strategic bankruptcy disguised as aggression.
The root cause of this self-inflicted wound lies in the Strait of Hormuz, the world's most vital energy chokepoint. After nearly six months of severe disruption triggered by the U.S.-Israeli military aggression against Iran, the waterway that once carried one-fifth of global oil and LNG supply has been reduced to a fraction of its normal flow. Daily transits have plummeted from 130 vessels to just a few, and war-risk insurance premiums have soared to 40 times normal levels. Hundreds of ships remain trapped in the Persian Gulf, and global oil flows have collapsed from 21 million barrels per day to a trickle. Iran, facing a U.S. naval blockade, has responded with controlled restrictions on the strait, creating a standoff that punishes everyone.
The economic devastation is global in scope. Asia, which historically received 80 to 90 percent of Hormuz-shipped oil and LNG, is enduring its largest energy shock in history. Japan, South Korea, India, Pakistan, and Bangladesh face crippling fuel shortages, soaring inflation, and industrial paralysis. European nations grapple with surging gas and electricity prices, while African countries dependent on food and energy imports confront acute shortages. The World Bank and institutions like Wood Mackenzie and Capital Economics warn that prolonged disruption could shave 0.5 to 1 percent off global GDP growth—a staggering blow to an already fragile world economy.
But perhaps the most telling consequence is the blowback on the United States itself. Trump's "maximum pressure" campaign has not broken Iran; it has made the regime more resilient. Airstrikes have weakened Iran militarily but strengthened its internal cohesion. The war has destroyed Iranian infrastructure and claimed lives, yet for most Americans, the conflict remains a distant abstraction—except at the gas pump, where prices have surged, and in the inflationary pressures now spreading through the U.S. economy. The SPR depletion is not a sign of American might; it is a warning that Washington has overextended itself and lost its ability to respond to future crises.
Trump's strategy rests on a fundamental misunderstanding of Iran. The Islamic Republic is simultaneously ideological and pragmatic. It resisted U.S. pressure for decades; it will not capitulate to coercion. Instead, by controlling the Strait of Hormuz, Tehran has demonstrated that it can impose reciprocal costs on its adversaries—and those costs are now painfully evident.
The administration's D-Day economic offensive is not a game-changer; it is a last gasp. Trump has repeated the same flawed playbook that has failed U.S. presidents since 1979: pressure as a substitute for strategy, military bluster as a cover for diplomatic bankruptcy. But this time, the consequences are not confined to Iran. The global economy is reeling, U.S. strategic reserves are depleted, and America's credibility is eroding with every empty threat. Far from breaking Iran, Trump's war has exposed the limits of American power and inflicted greater harm on the United States and its allies than on the intended target. The red light is flashing—not for Tehran, but for Washington.

articles.title: Zelenskyy comments on possible support from Ukraine in event of Russian attack on Baltic states
articles.body:
Zelenskyy comments on possible support from Ukraine in event of Russian attack on Baltic states
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has commented on the possibility of helping the Baltic states in the event of a potential Russian attack on them.
Source: Ukrainian news agency Ukrinform citing Zelenskyy during a joint press conference with his Estonian counterpart Alar Karis in Kyiv, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Asked whether Ukraine would send its troops in the event of an attack on Estonia, Zelenskyy said the Baltic states should be protected by NATO.
Quote: "As for our military, Ukraine is not in NATO. Estonia is in NATO. If we believe in the strength of NATO, then Estonia – God forbid, but if there are any risks – has more than 30 countries that, in my view, should simultaneously defend any country that is a NATO ally."
Background:
- Earlier, Reuters reported that Poland, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia are cooperating to shield their infrastructure from potential Russian attacks that could be staged as false-flag operations, as allied intelligence services have repeatedly warned.
- Last month, Lithuania deployed troops to reinforce special forces in order to secure its liquefied natural gas import terminal, oil products terminal, a key power line with Poland and the Kruonis Pumped Storage Hydroelectric Plant.
- Leaders of NATO's eastern flank countries have recently issued public warnings, citing intelligence indicating that Russia is preparing provocations on their territory.

articles.title: For first time, Ukraine is tendering ground robots to ministry-set specifications and no maker can take more than half of any class
articles.body:
Ukraine's ground robots ran more than 100,000 missions in the first eight months of 2026. The Defense Procurement Agency will now buy logistics and strike ground robotic complexes according to specifications set by the Defense Ministry, rather than approving models one at a time, the ministry announced.
The mechanism is three days old. The agency applied the same structure to fiber-optic FPV drones on 22 August—classes, multiple lots each, no supplier above half a class. Ukraine is standardizing how it buys entire weapons categories, one category at a time.
The rules sort makers by class
Complexes will be divided into classes by operating range and payload, with four to five lots per class. No single manufacturer may take more than half the order within one class.
Suppliers must meet the technical specifications and hold at least one codified ground robotic complex. The procurement runs in a closed environment under defense security requirements.
"A tender is one of the best instruments for this, because we can buy more equipment for the same money and minimize the risk of supply disruptions by splitting the order among different manufacturers," Deputy Defense Minister Mstyslav Banik said.
Mission volume keeps climbing
Monthly figures of ground robot missions logged in the DELTA combat system rose almost without interruption: 7,511 in January, 11,028 in April, 19,969 in July. Units recorded another 15,729 between 1 and 20 August, about 790 a day compared with roughly 640 a day in July, The Defense Post reported.
Ukraine has contracted more than 22,000 ground robots since January, nearly double the total for all of 2025. The number of units operating them grew from 117 at the end of 2025 to 230 by mid-2026.
A commander disputes the evacuation case
The ministry lists casualty evacuation as one of the tender's purposes. A frontline officer challenged that three days ago.
Tetiana Chornovol, who commands an anti-tank guided missile platoon, said ground robots are too slow for evacuation and often easy targets for Russian drones, arguing brigades need staffed evacuation teams and small light-armored vehicles instead.

articles.title: Iran replacing, producing new air defense systems
articles.body:
Iran's air defence chief said his force's performance in hitting enemy fighter jets and strategic drones had been demonstrated during the two recent wars, with lessons now feeding new tactics and locally built systems.
Brigadier General Alireza Elhami, commander of the army's air defence force, said the 12-day war had provided valuable experience that was applied during the 40-day war, where the effectiveness was more visible. "We hit a significant number of strategic and effective drones as well as enemy fighter aircraft," he said.
He said the 40-day war had produced important lessons in tactics, system production, deployment and layout, leading to changes. "We are now in a position where we are moving forward based on 100 percent Iranian capabilities. We are adding systems and replicating systems that performed well in the 40-day war," Elhami said.
"Based on our experience, we are producing new systems and equipment, all of it relying on 100 percent Iranian knowledge and expertise," he added.
MNA

articles.title: CIA chief was aboard mystery US C-17 flight to Moscow
articles.body:
We now know why a US Air Force C-17 made an unusual flight from Riga to Moscow: CIA Director John Ratcliffe was aboard the aircraft for meetings in the Russian capital.
The reason behind an unusual US Air Force C-17 Globemaster III flight into Moscow has now emerged, with CBS News reporting that CIA Director John Ratcliffe travelled aboard the aircraft for meetings in the Russian capital, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The development answers the central question raised when the aircraft appeared on civilian flight-tracking services earlier on 25 August. What initially looked like a highly unusual American military transport movement into Russia was, according to CBS News senior White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs, carrying the CIA Director on a visit to Moscow. Jacobs reported, citing sources, that Ratcliffe travelled to Russia aboard a C-17 for meetings in the city and said it appeared to be his first known trip to the country since becoming CIA Director, although he has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts.
It appears to be Ratcliffe’s first known trip to Russia as CIA director, though he has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts. https://t.co/J9ugJvGnSj
— Jennifer Jacobs (@JenniferJJacobs) August 25, 2026
The aircraft was identified through open-source flight data as US Air Force C-17A Globemaster III serial 07-7191, using the callsign REACH 4555. It had first been tracked leaving the Washington area for Riga on 23 August, before departing the Latvian capital two days later and heading east towards Moscow, a routing that immediately drew attention because direct movements by identifiable US military aircraft into Russia have become extremely uncommon amid the deterioration in relations between Washington and Moscow.
UK Defence Journal Senior Editor Jon, known as DefenceGeek on X, followed the movement as it developed, first noting the aircraft’s arrival in Riga and then its subsequent flight into Russia. Tracking data showed REACH 4555 approaching Moscow before video and photographs from the city showed a C-17 descending towards the Russian capital, confirming that the aircraft had completed the unusual journey.
At that stage, however, the aircraft itself offered little indication of what the mission involved. The C-17 is the US Air Force’s principal heavy strategic transport aircraft and is routinely used to move personnel, vehicles and outsized cargo over intercontinental distances, while REACH callsigns are commonly associated with US Air Mobility Command missions, meaning the route could be followed in public without revealing who was aboard or why the aircraft had been sent to Moscow.
The CBS reporting changes that picture considerably, placing the flight in the context of a senior US intelligence visit rather than an unexplained logistics movement. Ratcliffe’s reported presence also helps explain why a conspicuous military aircraft was being used on a route that would otherwise have appeared highly unusual, although the precise purpose of his meetings, the Russian officials he met and the subjects discussed have not been made public.
Separate activity around the flight had already suggested that the movement involved more than a routine cargo mission. Imagery circulating after the C-17 arrived appeared to show US government vehicles travelling in convoy through Moscow, with open-source observers pointing to registration plates that appeared consistent with Latvia-issued diplomatic plates. The timing now makes a connection with Ratcliffe’s visit more plausible, although the available imagery does not establish whether those vehicles carried the CIA Director, formed part of his security detail or had any direct connection with the delegation.
There was also additional US government aviation activity at Riga before REACH 4555 continued to Moscow. A Boeing C-40, serial 02-0042 and using the callsign REACH 790, was tracked arriving at Riga International Airport from Joint Base Andrews on 23 August, with open-source imagery suggesting that it was parked close to the C-17. That movement can now be viewed alongside Ratcliffe’s reported journey, but there is still no confirmation that the C-40 continued to Russia or that it played a direct role in the CIA Director’s visit.
Jacobs’ reporting that Ratcliffe has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts is also significant because it indicates that direct intelligence channels between Washington and Moscow have continued despite the wider breakdown in political and military relations. What those contacts have covered remains unknown, and there is no public information establishing whether the Moscow meetings concerned Ukraine, detainees, strategic stability, intelligence liaison or another issue.
The known sequence is now considerably clearer than it was when REACH 4555 first appeared over Russia: the aircraft travelled from the United States to Riga, later flew onward to Moscow, and was subsequently identified by CBS News sources as carrying the CIA Director for meetings in the Russian capital. The reason for the flight is therefore no longer the mystery it was when the movement was first detected, even if the substance of Ratcliffe’s discussions remains undisclosed.
The US Air Force declined to comment when approached about the flight, while no detailed public account of Ratcliffe’s meetings has yet been issued by the CIA or Russian authorities. What remains unanswered is not why an American C-17 was in Moscow, but what brought the CIA Director there and what was discussed once he arrived.

articles.title: CIA chief was aboard mystery US C-17 flight to Moscow
articles.body:
We now know why a US Air Force C-17 made an unusual flight from Riga to Moscow: CIA Director John Ratcliffe was aboard the aircraft for meetings in the Russian capital.
The reason behind an unusual US Air Force C-17 Globemaster III flight into Moscow has now emerged, with CBS News reporting that CIA Director John Ratcliffe travelled aboard the aircraft for meetings in the Russian capital, the UK Defence Journal understands.
The development answers the central question raised when the aircraft appeared on civilian flight-tracking services earlier on 25 August. What initially looked like a highly unusual American military transport movement into Russia was, according to CBS News senior White House reporter Jennifer Jacobs, carrying the CIA Director on a visit to Moscow. Jacobs reported, citing sources, that Ratcliffe travelled to Russia aboard a C-17 for meetings in the city and said it appeared to be his first known trip to the country since becoming CIA Director, although he has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts.
It appears to be Ratcliffe’s first known trip to Russia as CIA director, though he has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts. https://t.co/J9ugJvGnSj
— Jennifer Jacobs (@JenniferJJacobs) August 25, 2026
The aircraft was identified through open-source flight data as US Air Force C-17A Globemaster III serial 07-7191, using the callsign REACH 4555. It had first been tracked leaving the Washington area for Riga on 23 August, before departing the Latvian capital two days later and heading east towards Moscow, a routing that immediately drew attention because direct movements by identifiable US military aircraft into Russia have become extremely uncommon amid the deterioration in relations between Washington and Moscow.
UK Defence Journal Senior Editor Jon, known as DefenceGeek on X, followed the movement as it developed, first noting the aircraft’s arrival in Riga and then its subsequent flight into Russia. Tracking data showed REACH 4555 approaching Moscow before video and photographs from the city showed a C-17 descending towards the Russian capital, confirming that the aircraft had completed the unusual journey.
At that stage, however, the aircraft itself offered little indication of what the mission involved. The C-17 is the US Air Force’s principal heavy strategic transport aircraft and is routinely used to move personnel, vehicles and outsized cargo over intercontinental distances, while REACH callsigns are commonly associated with US Air Mobility Command missions, meaning the route could be followed in public without revealing who was aboard or why the aircraft had been sent to Moscow.
The CBS reporting changes that picture considerably, placing the flight in the context of a senior US intelligence visit rather than an unexplained logistics movement. Ratcliffe’s reported presence also helps explain why a conspicuous military aircraft was being used on a route that would otherwise have appeared highly unusual, although the precise purpose of his meetings, the Russian officials he met and the subjects discussed have not been made public.
Separate activity around the flight had already suggested that the movement involved more than a routine cargo mission. Imagery circulating after the C-17 arrived appeared to show US government vehicles travelling in convoy through Moscow, with open-source observers pointing to registration plates that appeared consistent with Latvia-issued diplomatic plates. The timing now makes a connection with Ratcliffe’s visit more plausible, although the available imagery does not establish whether those vehicles carried the CIA Director, formed part of his security detail or had any direct connection with the delegation.
There was also additional US government aviation activity at Riga before REACH 4555 continued to Moscow. A Boeing C-40, serial 02-0042 and using the callsign REACH 790, was tracked arriving at Riga International Airport from Joint Base Andrews on 23 August, with open-source imagery suggesting that it was parked close to the C-17. That movement can now be viewed alongside Ratcliffe’s reported journey, but there is still no confirmation that the C-40 continued to Russia or that it played a direct role in the CIA Director’s visit.
Jacobs’ reporting that Ratcliffe has maintained contact with Russian intelligence counterparts is also significant because it indicates that direct intelligence channels between Washington and Moscow have continued despite the wider breakdown in political and military relations. What those contacts have covered remains unknown, and there is no public information establishing whether the Moscow meetings concerned Ukraine, detainees, strategic stability, intelligence liaison or another issue.
The known sequence is now considerably clearer than it was when REACH 4555 first appeared over Russia: the aircraft travelled from the United States to Riga, later flew onward to Moscow, and was subsequently identified by CBS News sources as carrying the CIA Director for meetings in the Russian capital. The reason for the flight is therefore no longer the mystery it was when the movement was first detected, even if the substance of Ratcliffe’s discussions remains undisclosed.
The US Air Force declined to comment when approached about the flight, while no detailed public account of Ratcliffe’s meetings has yet been issued by the CIA or Russian authorities. What remains unanswered is not why an American C-17 was in Moscow, but what brought the CIA Director there and what was discussed once he arrived.

articles.title: U.S. Navy awards Castelion $90 million for hypersonic weapon
articles.body:
- The Navy awarded Castelion $89,997,162 to advance the Blackbeard hypersonic weapon to Early Operational Capability, funding 50 weapons.
- The order supports Blackbeard's transition to a Navy Program of Record and includes work to speed potential exports to allies.
The U.S. Navy awarded Castelion Corp. nearly $90 million to advance its Blackbeard hypersonic strike weapon toward Early Operational Capability, the company announced August 25.
The order funds engineering, technical, logistics and manufacturing work supporting 50 early operational capability weapons and the missile’s transition to a formal Navy Program of Record.
The contract also funds Defense Exportability Features, design modifications intended to speed up potential sales to U.S. allies and partners. Work will be performed in Torrance, California, and is expected to be completed by August 2028.
The order falls under a Small Business Innovation Research Phase III effort tied to the topic “Low Cost Highly Manufacturable Long Range Strike Weapon Production.” Naval Air Warfare Center Aircraft Division in Lakehurst, New Jersey, is the contracting activity, and the action was not competitively bid. Funding includes $50 million in fiscal 2026 defense-wide research funds, roughly $15.8 million in fiscal 2026 Navy research funds, and about $24.2 million in fiscal 2025 Navy research funds, the last of which expires at the end of the current fiscal year.
Blackbeard is designed to fly faster than Mach 5 while maneuvering within the atmosphere, built for both air launch from aircraft such as the F/A-18 and a parallel ground-launched variant compatible with HIMARS. The Navy selected Blackbeard in February as the first weapon candidate under its Multi-mission Affordable Capacity Effector program, known as MACE, which aims to field large quantities of lower-cost, longer-range strike weapons rather than relying solely on smaller numbers of expensive, exquisite systems. The Navy confirmed that link in April, tying the missile to a rapid prototyping effort structured within the fiscal 2026 Navy research budget as part of its Precision Strike Weapons Development Program.
Castelion has received a rapid sequence of expanding Navy contracts for Blackbeard over the past year, each building on the last. Following initial integration awards from the Army and Navy in October 2025, the Navy awarded the company nearly $50 million in February 2026 to fund full-scale prototypes and flight testing at Point Mugu Sea Range. That was followed in April by a $105 million contract modification to integrate the missile onto the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet and support live-fire testing in the Indo-Pacific Command area of responsibility, with work expected to run through January 2028. In June, the Navy ordered 50 early operational capability pre-production prototypes and 50 storage and shipping containers under a $23.4 million contract, the first production-style delivery order for a low-cost hypersonic weapon of its kind. Roughly three-quarters of that work went to Castelion’s Project Ranger manufacturing campus, a 1,000-acre hypersonic production site in Rio Rancho, New Mexico, with the remainder handled at the company’s Torrance headquarters.
Castelion was founded in 2022 by Bryon Hargis, Sean Pitt and Andrew Kreitz, all of whom previously worked at SpaceX. The company describes Blackbeard as the first U.S. hypersonic system engineered from inception for industrial-rate output and commercial-style unit costs, built around continuous flight test iteration rather than the long, singular test campaigns typical of legacy hypersonic programs. Castelion has said its longer-term ambition includes multi-year procurement of 500 weapons annually, a production rate intended to shift the program from a development effort into fielded capability at scale. The company operates manufacturing sites in New Mexico, Texas and California, along with offices in Washington, D.C.
Congress increased MACE program funding by more than $140 million in the fiscal 2026 defense appropriations act, more than doubling the program’s base funding, though lawmakers did not specify how the additional money should be spent. Early budget documents for fiscal 2027 show continued funding growth planned for the broader Precision Strike Weapons Development Program that houses MACE.

articles.title: North Korea sharpens anti-Japan rhetoric as Russia ties grow
articles.body:
North Korea has stepped up its verbal attacks on Japan, issuing more than a dozen denunciations through state media since early July and hardening its rhetoric in recent days by accusing Tokyo of whipping up a “neo-militarist frenzy” and preparing for a “war of aggression”.
Analysts said the latest broadsides from Kim Jong-un’s regime reflected both renewed confidence in Pyongyang as ties with Moscow deepen, and a desire to frame Asia-Pacific geopolitics as a contest between rival blocs – mirroring the Nato-Warsaw Pact stand-off at the height of the Cold War.
The attacks come amid rising tensions across the region: North Korea is forging deeper security and economic ties with Russia, Beijing is increasingly at odds with Tokyo, and Japan is moving to strengthen its defence posture in response to perceived threats from the other three.
“Both Russia and China have problems in their relationships with Japan at the moment and North Korea is keen to participate in the criticisms of Tokyo,” said Andrei Lankov, a Russian-born professor of history and international relations at Seoul’s Kookmin University.
“It is important for the regime to have an ‘evil enemy’ that they can complain about and Japan meets that need,” he said. “Pyongyang is very keen to side with Russia and China, as it helps to promote the narrative that they are part of a mighty military bloc.”
Such a bloc is unlikely to materialise any time soon, but analysts say that will not stop Pyongyang from launching further provocations to unsettle Tokyo.
On Monday, Pyongyang’s state-run Korea Central News Agency (KCNA) accused Japanese politicians of “harbouring militaristic ambitions” after they paid respects to the nation’s 2.5 million war dead at Tokyo’s Yasukuni Shrine, which also honours 1,066 men convicted of war crimes.

articles.title: ADF neutralizes 134 Russian drones used to attack Ukraine overnight
articles.body:
ADF neutralizes 134 Russian drones used to attack Ukraine overnight
According to Ukrinform, the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported this on Telegram.
Starting at 18:00 on August 25, Russian forces attacked Ukraine with 162 Shahed-type attack UAVs, including jet-powered variants, as well as Gerbera drones and Parody-type decoy drones. They were launched from the areas of Kursk, Orel, and Primorsko-Akhtarsk in Russia, as well as the temporarily occupied Donetsk and Hvardiiske in the temporarily occupied Crimea.
The aerial attack was repelled by Ukrainian aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare units, unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine's Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00 on Wednesday, August 26, Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 134 drones over the northern, southern, and eastern regions of the country.
Hits were recorded at 18 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at three locations.
The attack is ongoing, with several enemy drones still in Ukrainian airspace.
As Ukrinform previously reported, on the morning of August 26, a woman and a four-year-old child were killed in Chernihiv as a result of a Russian drone attack. A 14-year-old child was also injured.

articles.title: US targets 1,000-plus Tomahawks a year
articles.body:
Raytheon has received a seven-year contract worth $22.9 billion to sharply increase Tomahawk cruise missile production, with annual output planned to rise above 1,000 weapons for the US Navy and allied customers.
The United States is moving to raise annual production of Tomahawk long-range cruise missiles to more than 1,000 weapons under a seven-year contract awarded to Raytheon, according to the company.
The RTX news update values the agreement at $22.9 billion, approximately £16.8 billion, and says it will support a major expansion of manufacturing capacity for the US Navy and allied customers. Raytheon described the award as part of the Department of War’s wider “Arsenal of Freedom” effort to increase production of high-demand weapons.
Tomahawk is a long-range, subsonic precision-strike cruise missile used primarily to attack targets on land from substantial stand-off distances. In US naval service it can be launched from surface warships and submarines, giving commanders the ability to strike fixed and other designated targets hundreds of miles from the launch platform without placing crewed aircraft directly over the target area. Newer versions of the weapon have also expanded the missile’s targeting and maritime strike capabilities.
Raytheon President Phil Jasper said, as quoted in a news update: “Tomahawk is the Navy’s most important strike weapon, able to target hostile forces hundreds of miles away without ever risking the lives of our sailors.”
He added: “We are making significant investments in our workforce, technology, supply chain and facilities to dramatically boost production capacity and meet surging demand.”
The scale of the planned production increase is substantial. RTX said the new contract supports an annual manufacturing rate exceeding 1,000 Tomahawks, together with associated support. The company did not state that production is already running at that level, instead describing the figure as the target of the multi-year production ramp.
RTX has already been increasing deliveries. According to the company, Raytheon delivered three times as many Tomahawk missiles during the first half of 2026 as it did during the equivalent six months of 2025. The seven-year arrangement is intended to provide greater certainty to the manufacturer and its supply chain as production expands further.
Hundreds of small and medium-sized suppliers across the United States are expected to contribute to the programme. Long-term contracting can allow manufacturers further down the weapons supply chain to invest in machinery, staff and production capacity with greater confidence than under smaller annual orders, particularly where specialist components can otherwise become bottlenecks as final assembly rates increase.
Tomahawk has been in US service for decades and has been repeatedly used in combat for long-range conventional strikes. The weapon has undergone successive upgrades rather than being replaced outright, with later variants introducing changes to communications, targeting and mission flexibility while retaining the basic role of delivering precision effects at extended range.

articles.title: BNN Interview | Cargo does not disappear — it goes to competitors. Latvia is losing millions and its place on the transit map
articles.body:
Ilona Bērziņa
Latvia’s ports are still financing themselves, while the railway is already being supported by taxpayers. A shortage of funding is not the industry’s only problem — Latvia is also losing competitiveness, partly as a result of policies the country itself has adopted. Ivars Landmanis, Chairman of the Board of the Latvian Stevedoring Companies Association (LSA), says the greatest concern is that one more relatively minor shock to the transport and logistics sector could trigger an irreversible “domino effect.”
What exactly would this “domino effect” look like? Could it mean insolvency among port companies?
A “domino effect” is a chain reaction in which one event or action triggers a series of subsequent events that may have far-reaching consequences. A port’s revenues decline, terminals no longer have sufficient funds to maintain infrastructure, prolonged legal disputes over unpaid port dues may begin, followed by collective redundancies, and ultimately even environmental problems.
Once a port can no longer afford to maintain its waters, the required depths for vessels to enter the port, and the rest of its infrastructure, we can forget about NATO vessels — as well as other large ships — calling at Latvian ports. It is far easier to prevent such a situation than to deal later with the consequences of politicians’ lack of foresight and inaction.
Moreover, if businesses operating in ports go bankrupt, who will support the families of their employees and the small businesses that depend on them — hair salons, cafés, small shops and other service providers? Perhaps instead we should be thinking about how, under certain circumstances, to support the ports and restructure the railway.
Why must businesses constantly fight the “windmills” of bureaucracy and try to understand where the hidden pitfalls of policymaking lie, instead of simply being allowed to work and generate revenue for the state? If politicians are so determined to hinder normal economic development, ultimately creating a situation in which ports and the railway have to be subsidised, then they should say openly that taxpayers will have to pay for their inability to make economically sound decisions — decisions that may not please Brussels or certain populist parties, but would benefit Latvia.
Latvia has the Latvian Ports, Transit and Logistics Council, whose main task is to coordinate state policy in the sector. Is it actually doing so?
Since the Council is chaired by the Prime Minister, it could indeed serve as a forum for discussing all the sector’s pressing issues. However, in recent years, Council meetings have been held unacceptably infrequently. Although its regulations require meetings to be held at least once every quarter, only five Council meetings have taken place from 2024 through the 18th of August of this year.
At a time when the industry is undergoing one of the most rapid structural transformations since the restoration of Latvia’s independence — with declining cargo volumes from Russia, Belarus and Central Asia, falling rail freight volumes, revenue problems at ports, and the need to find entirely new markets — we have lacked a comprehensive sectoral policy document that would also set out specific measures for dealing with declining cargo volumes.
Back in 2014, auditing firm EY concluded that if Latvia were to lose Russian and Belarusian cargo, it would lose 1.4 billion euros in turnover, GDP would decline by 1.9%, employment by 1.7%, and tax revenues by 2.6%. In that same year, 2014, before the decline in coal, petroleum products and rail freight began, transit from Russia and Belarus alone generated approximately 174 million euros in annual tax revenue.
However, already in the early 2000s, when Russia began building and expanding its Baltic Sea ports — Ust-Luga, Primorsk and Vysotsk — it was clear that the economic objective was to avoid paying Latvian, Estonian or Lithuanian ports and railways for handling Russian exports and instead route those exports through Russia’s own infrastructure.
For all these years, businesses operating in Latvian ports have been knocking on the doors of successive governments, calling for railway tariffs and other issues to be addressed in a way that would allow us to remain competitive and therefore attractive, including for cargo from Central Asian countries. Yet our appeals have fallen on deaf ears.
As a result, in 2025 and 2026 the state allocated almost 90 million euros annually to maintain public railway infrastructure and ensure the financial balance of Latvijas dzelzceļš (LDz). If declining cargo volumes mean that the infrastructure of Latvia’s major ports also has to be financed from the state budget, total support could exceed 110 million euros per year.
The United States has lifted sanctions on the transit of Belarusian mineral fertilisers, while the European Union has not. Russia is benefiting, earning approximately 500 million euros annually from these cargoes alone. Does Latvia have any opportunity to influence the EU’s common regulatory framework regarding Belarusian mineral fertilisers?
The objective of the sanctions is understandable — to reduce Belarus’s revenues and its ability to support Russia’s war in Ukraine. However, we need to assess whether the sanctions are actually achieving this objective.
Belarusian mineral fertiliser exports have not stopped. Instead, a large proportion of these cargoes has been redirected to Russian railways and ports, amounting to approximately 11–12 million tonnes per year.
If even five million tonnes of Belarusian mineral fertilisers per year were routed through Latvia, our economy could gain at least 100 million euros annually through railway services, terminals, port services, taxes and related industries.
Within the Russian transport corridor, the amount is considerably higher — Russian railway and port logistics for Belarusian mineral fertilisers cost approximately 47–59 euros per tonne. It can be predicted with reasonable confidence that, for purely economic reasons, Belarusian businesses would much prefer to route these cargoes through the Baltic States, but sanctions currently prevent them from doing so.
We therefore believe that the EU should assess whether the current policy is achieving its intended objective and whether its side effects are generating greater economic benefits for Russia than for Europe.
Sanctions decisions are taken jointly by all EU Member States, so the Latvian government can initiate a review of the regulatory framework, submit assessments of the economic and security impacts, and seek support from other Member States. One option worth considering could be strictly controlled transit to third countries, with full traceability of cargoes and payments.
The key is to ensure that sanctions achieve their security objective rather than merely shifting cargo flows and revenues from European ports to Russia.
The Port of Ventspils is particularly exposed to fluctuations in certain major cargo categories — petroleum products, Kazakh coal and other shipments along the eastern corridor. What should be done to encourage Kazakhstan, for example, to route its coal through Ventspils? Is this primarily a question of railway tariffs, or are there other factors?
Railway tariffs are one of the key issues, but they are not the only one. Kazakh businesses assess the total cost of the entire route, from the point of origin to the final buyer.
The calculation includes railway tariffs, terminal services, port and shipping costs, the speed of customs and border controls, as well as the security and predictability of the entire route. Ultimately, the decision is always based on a business calculation — whether transporting cargo through Latvia is cheaper, faster and safer than using an alternative route.
If we want to preserve the economic contribution of our ports, jobs, import and export services, as well as military mobility capabilities, Latvia’s transport corridor must remain competitive.
What, in your view, should be done to stimulate business activity related to transport and logistics, including transit?
We simply need to understand that the domestic economy does not generate enough business for all of Latvia’s ports, and that the volume of cargo generated within the region is insufficient to sustain either terminal operations or port infrastructure.
Many people ask why the transit sector does not cooperate more closely with Ukraine. Intensive efforts were made to develop such cooperation, but unfortunately, given the current rail connection between Latvia and Ukraine — via Lithuania and Poland — significant cargo flows are not feasible.
First, there are differences in railway gauges, which require additional operations involving cargo or railway wagons. Second, capacity is limited. All of this slows cargo delivery times and increases costs.
Consequently, intensive cooperation between Latvian ports and Ukraine can only develop once the railway connection through Belarus is reopened. Latvian politicians must also take this into account if, as a country, we genuinely want to become practically involved in helping Ukraine with its post-war reconstruction.
Business can be stimulated in several ways. For example, policymakers should refrain from making populist decisions without first consulting the industry and understanding the economic consequences of those decisions. Unfortunately, several political forces have acted in precisely this way, causing an enormous negative impact on Latvia’s economy.
Secondly, all bureaucratic obstacles should be reviewed. For example, the process for obtaining various permits needs to become more flexible so that terminals can quickly adapt to handling different types of cargo. This is particularly important in the liquid bulk cargo segment, where switching from one type of cargo to another is technologically complex, time-consuming and expensive.
If obtaining approval for the necessary amendments to environmental permits takes almost a year, we lose competitiveness in the eyes of our customers. The state should therefore provide a more accommodating and flexible approach — shortening procedural deadlines, reviewing requirements and introducing “green corridors” for strategically important projects.
Thirdly, we need to assess how to become more competitive in terms of tariffs. We could experiment with the excise duty on diesel fuel used for rail freight and with infrastructure fee discounts for certain types of cargo.
For example, Estonia, in an effort to attract Kazakh grain, was prepared to reduce railway infrastructure charges. We also need to experiment — there is no reason why a discount would have to remain in place indefinitely. We could introduce it for a limited period and see whether it works. If cargo volumes return, the terms could then be reviewed.
We respect European Union sanctions. However, it is no secret that they have an impact on border countries and the businesses operating in them. How easy or difficult is it, under these circumstances, to find business partners willing to cooperate with us and invest here?
It is very difficult. Our region is becoming increasingly unattractive. Stability, predictability and cargo security are extremely important. The political and public climate is also a problem. How many times have politicians talked about closing the border? At the same time, we travel to Central Asian countries, try to build cooperation and invest energy and other resources in attracting cargo.
As soon as someone publicly announces that we are about to close the border or dismantle the railway tracks, that information immediately reaches our partners, and they call us asking what is going on. Latvia itself creates a sense of instability, and this benefits our neighbours — cargo is redirected to Lithuania or elsewhere. There is no consistency or clear strategic direction. With one hand, politicians are trying to build relationships in Central Asia, while with the other they are saying: let’s close the border or dismantle the railway tracks. How are businesses supposed to operate under such conditions?
More than 70% of Latvia’s state oil reserves are stored within Latvia, while the remaining 30% are stored in other EU countries. Would it perhaps make more sense to store all of Latvia’s state reserves within the country itself?
At present, reserves are secured for 92 days, and every fuel consumer pays approximately 7–8 cents from every litre purchased towards the establishment and maintenance of these fuel reserves. As of the 1st of January, 2026, the official fee is 81.26 euros per tonne of petroleum products, and it is currently the most expensive system in the Baltic States.
Historically, we purchased only so-called “option contracts” — essentially the right to purchase fuel from traders in the event of a crisis. The state is now changing this system and is gradually purchasing fuel into physical state ownership over a five-year period.
At present, the greatest concern is why there is so little information available about these state reserve procurements and why responsibility for them has been entrusted to the public asset manager Possessor, where the final decision is made by just one person. In my view, this is highly risky, because the decisions involve sums amounting to hundreds of millions of euros. At the same time, open tenders are not organised for security reasons.
The same applies to the rental of storage tanks in which state-owned fuel reserves are stored. It is unclear what principles are used to select these facilities. There are no open tenders; instead, market research is conducted. It has been reported publicly that the average rental price under the contracts concluded is 5 euros per tonne. However, according to information available to me, some terminals offered significantly, significantly lower prices, yet no contracts were concluded with them.
What is the explanation for this, and why should the state overpay if cheaper offers are available on the market? If the reserve manager’s choices when awarding storage contracts are not transparent or understandable, this creates an unequal situation and unfair competitive conditions among terminals.
What are currently the biggest problems facing the industry, and what solutions are possible?
Stevedoring companies are service providers. For the industry to operate, it needs customers and cargo. At present, there is considerably less cargo due both to sanctions and the broader geopolitical situation. If there is no cargo, there is nothing to handle, so the main objective is to ensure that cargo continues to flow through Latvia.
We, as port operators, are working simultaneously in several directions — strengthening cooperation with Central Asian countries, seeking new cargo flows in Europe and Scandinavia, working to attract industrial projects and investors, and assessing solutions to reduce railway and overall transportation costs.
A clear and stable governance model, as well as predictable funding for critical infrastructure, is also essential for the development of the ports. Latvia’s ports contain infrastructure of national importance, and several port companies perform essential functions in supporting Latvia’s economy and national security.
At present, one major global problem is unpredictability. Rules, tariffs, sanctions regimes and border operations frequently change across the region, making it difficult for customers to plan their activities over the long term. In the transport business, good infrastructure alone is not enough — customers need to know that a route will remain safe, cost-effective and accessible over the long term.
And there is one more point: when decisions are being made about an industry that is already balancing on the brink of survival, policymakers need to talk to the industry. During the budget process, the government cannot simply increase the natural resources tax, excise duty or other charges without first determining whether the sector is capable of bearing the additional burden.
Otherwise, we end up in a vicious circle: the budget forecasts higher revenues from increased taxes, but cargo volumes do not increase — on the contrary, they may decline. Taxes can be raised indefinitely, but if there is no cargo, there will be no revenue either.
The state should therefore develop a model in which reasonable rates attract cargo and generate real revenue, rather than continuing to raise rates until cargo simply goes elsewhere.

articles.title: Iran and Oman discuss temporary Hormuz corridor
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Iran and Oman discuss temporary Hormuz corridor as impasse with US drags on
Iran said it had restarted talks with neighbor Oman to manage the Strait of Hormuz as it faces heightened economic pressure from US President Donald Trump in the wider conflict.
Iran and Oman have been in on-and-off talks for weeks about controlling traffic through the strategic waterway, which handled one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments before the war began in February. Most shipping has been shut down since then.
The two countries said on Tuesday that they discussed "a joint temporary navigational corridor" through the strait and agreed to clear it of mines.
Trump said all mines in the strait had been cleared, repeating comments that he has previously made. Though active hostilities between the U.S. and Iran have largely subsided, diplomatic efforts to reach a peace deal have stalled and passage through the waterway remains perilous.
An oil tanker was struck on Tuesday by an unidentified projectile and disabled about 9 nautical miles (17 km) northeast of Oman's Ash Shishah, which lies at the entrance to the strait, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said.
Separately, the U.S. Secret Service said on Tuesday that it was aware of a video broadcast by Iranian state television discussing a potential plot to assassinate Trump's youngest son, Barron.
A three-minute video broadcast by Iranian state TV discussed a potential plot to assassinate Barron Trump, 20, claiming that he was being monitored and alleging that a $10 million bounty had been offered for his killing. '
SANCTIONS
Despite the ongoing tensions, the U.S. is beginning to send personnel back to some diplomatic missions in the Middle East that were evacuated or downsized amid tensions with Iran, two people familiar with the matter told Reuters.
The move suggests Washington sees a lower risk of the conflict with Iran escalating in the near term, though some embassies will initially operate below full capacity. In an effort to hobble Iran's economy, the United States earlier this week threatened to punish countries that continue to do business with Iran, but said it would not impose penalties immediately.
Oil prices fell for a second day as traders brushed off the impact of the U.S. sanctions, while Iran denounced the U.S. effort to isolate its economy as an act of "gross lawlessness", expressing confidence that many countries would not join the pressure campaign
U.S. public approval of the war has fallen to its lowest level since the conflict's early days, and Trump's popularity is likewise at a record low ahead of congressional elections in November, according to Reuters/Ipsos polling.
Thousands of people have died in the conflict, most of them in Iran and Lebanon, while the U.S. and Israel have degraded much of Iran's conventional military capacity. The exact state of its nuclear program, which the U.S. and Israel aim to dismantle, remains unknown.

articles.title: Bail set for ex-Zelensky aide accused of money laundering
articles.body:
Bail set for ex-Zelensky aide accused of money laundering
Ukraine’s top anti-corruption court has set bail for the former deputy head of Vladimir Zelensky’s office, Irina Mudraya, at under $450,000 – less than one-seventh of the amount requested by prosecutors. She is suspected of channeling illicit funds into a bail payment for a defendant in a separate corruption case.
The High Anti-Corruption Court ruled on Tuesday that Mudraya must remain in Kiev and comply with any summons even if she posts bail, which she said she intends to do with the assistance of unnamed sponsors.
Zelensky fired Mudraya last week after she was formally accused of laundering about $3.3 million in cash to pay bail for former Energy Minister Herman Galushchenko. The latter had previously been implicated in an alleged $100 million kickback scheme blamed on Timur Mindich, a longtime associate of the Ukrainian leader.
The National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), two agencies established under Western pressure to tackle government graft, accused Mudraya of pressuring financial-monitoring officials to overlook suspicious transfers through Sense Bank. The lender was formerly the Ukrainian branch of Russia’s Alfa Bank before being nationalized by Kiev in 2023.
Surveillance recordings previously leaked to Ukrainian media suggested that Mindich’s group was interested in placing loyal figures on Sense Bank’s cabinet-appointed supervisory board. Ukrainian media dubbed Mindich “Zelensky’s bagman” amid suspicions that he was merely a frontman for corruption at the highest levels of government.
Mudraya trained as a lawyer specializing in banking and worked for several major clients in the sector before becoming a deputy justice minister in 2022. She moved to Zelensky’s office in 2024, ostensibly to contribute to Kiev’s efforts to obtain war reparations from Russia.
The former Zelensky aide has also been accused of participating in criminal schemes intended to expropriate real estate in Kiev worth some $16.75 million by illegally altering government records and pressuring judges to deny the legitimate owners legal recourse.
NABU and SAPO presented extensive records of conversations reportedly involving Mudraya and other suspects. The exchanges were allegedly recorded by former lawmaker and banker Maksim Mikitas.
Ukrainian media have speculated that Mikitas agreed to participate in the sting operation in return for leniency in other criminal cases being investigated by the two agencies.
During the bail hearings, Mudraya blamed a provocateur, apparently referring to Mikitas, for abusing her trust in order to produce incriminating recordings. She suggested that references to her alleged involvement in corruption were false but did not explain why she had failed to challenge the statements at the time.
Her defense team called several character witnesses, including Jonathan Markovitch, the chief rabbi of Kiev. He told the court that he knew Mudraya as a trustworthy member of the Jewish community and did not consider her a flight risk.
Mindich fled to Israel in November 2025, reportedly hours before he was due to be arrested. One of his key associates, Aleksandr Zukerman, also left for Israel. Both suspects hold Israeli citizenship.

articles.title: Ukraine hits Russian electronic warfare systems in Luhansk and Crimea, as well as depots in Zaporizhzhia Oblast
articles.body:
Ukraine hits Russian electronic warfare systems in Luhansk and Crimea, as well as depots in Zaporizhzhia Oblast
Ukraine's defence forces struck Russian electronic warfare systems in occupied Luhansk and in the village of Myrnyi in Crimea on 24 August and on the night of 24-25 August, as well as fuel, ammunition and logistics depots in Berdiansk and Prymorsk in Zaporizhzhia Oblast.
Source: General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine
Quote: "A specialised Peresvet-M electronic warfare system was struck in Luhansk.
A Starlink satellite communications jamming station was also struck in Myrnyi (temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea)."
Details: In Berdiansk, Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Ukraine's defence forces struck a Russian fuel, lubricants and ammunition depot, while in Prymorsk, logistics depots belonging to one of the Russian units were hit.
In addition, data analysis has confirmed the damage to a Russian MiG-29 fighter jet at the Millerovo airfield in Russia's Rostov Oblast on 24 August.
The extent of the damage inflicted on Russian forces is being assessed.
Background: Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces (USF) reported that on the night of 23-24 August they struck Russian logistics centres belonging to Ozon marketplace, a Russian multirole MiG-29 fighter jet and dozens of other targets in Russia and in the temporarily occupied territories.
